concepts.angle: STORY-FIRST: the product is a scrollable biography of one spot on Earth, told ring by ring (house -> block -> street -> neighborhood -> city -> county -> state -> country -> continent/plate). The map is a companion "postcard" that pulls back as you read, never the hero. The time control is a chapter dial: it re-issues the whole biography for a different date rather than scrubbing a map. Every design decision below optimises for (a) reading on a phone, (b) honest, warm handling of thin or missing data, and (c) a static site with no keys.
name_ideas: Snowball (small to big; matches the repo name sno-ball, and the 700-million-year 'Snowball Earth' chapter is a built-in in-joke)
concepts.concept:
You type a street address and the page turns into a long story you read by scrolling, like the biography of that exact spot. It starts with the smallest thing (the house itself), then widens one ring at a time: the block, the street, the neighborhood, the town, the county, the state, the country, the continent, and finally the rock under the floorboards and where that rock has travelled across the planet. Each ring is a short chapter: a title, a few paragraphs, one photo when there is one, and a line saying where the words came from. At the very top, a one-sentence biography sums the whole thing up ("A 1920s house on Maple Street, in a city founded in 1851, sitting on 300-million-year-old sandstone that was once at the equator"), so even when the house chapter is thin, the opening lands.

A small map "postcard" sits pinned at the top of the phone screen. It is not the main event. As you scroll from the house chapter to the city chapter to the continent chapter, the postcard quietly zooms out to match, so reading feels like a camera pulling back from your front door into space. Tap the postcard if you want the big map; otherwise just keep reading.

At the bottom of the screen is the time dial. Drag it back and the biography is re-told for that date: 1890, the year 1000, twenty thousand years ago, sixty-six million years ago. Chapters that did not exist yet say so plainly ("Not yet. This city will be founded in 1851, 59 years from now") instead of going blank, and the far-back chapters fold together into "The land", "The rock", and "Where this spot was on the globe". The dial has gears (years, decades, centuries, millennia, ice ages, millions, eons) so it is usable from last year to the birth of the Earth, and a "Chapters" list lets you jump straight to the famous moments (the dinosaurs' last day, Pangaea, Snowball Earth).

Honesty is part of the charm. Wikipedia knows a lot about cities and countries and almost nothing about individual houses, so the house and block chapters are usually thin. The site shows them as thin rings, says what it does know (the building's footprint, what the street is named after, the oldest buildings nearby), and nudges you outward: "The street has more". Friends who get the link on their phones should be able to read it in two minutes, flick back in time, and share their own address in one tap.

screens.name: Front Door
screens.description: Single-purpose landing. One large text field ('Type an address'), a Go button, a 'Use my location' button (browser geolocation -> reverse geocode), and three example addresses as tappable chips so the owner's friends can try it without typing. No autocomplete dropdown (OpenStreetMap's Nominatim usage policy forbids autocomplete; the field submits on Enter/Go only). Below the fold: a two-line explanation and the attribution footer. If Nominatim returns several candidates, an inline list appears ('Did you mean...') with the full display name of each. If it returns none: 'We couldn't find that address. Try adding the city or postcode.' The result URL is shareable: /#/story?q=<address>&at=now.

screens.name: The Story (main scroll)
screens.description: The core screen. Layout top to bottom on phone: (1) a 56px sticky header with the short address, the current date chip (tap to open the Time Dial), and a 32px tree-ring glyph showing which ring you are reading; (2) the 180px sticky map postcard that zooms with the current ring; (3) the Hero card with the one-sentence biography for the chosen date and a 'what we found / what we didn't' summary line ('Rich: city, state, country. Thin: house, block.'); (4) one chapter card per ring, small to big, each with an eyebrow ('RING 3 - YOUR STREET'), a title, 1-4 paragraphs, an optional photo, a mini facts strip (founded, population then, name then), and source chips; (5) the Deep Time chapters ('The land', 'The rock under your house', 'Where this spot was', 'Life here then'); (6) an End card with 'Flip back in time' and 'Share this spot' buttons. The Time Dial is a collapsed bottom sheet (96px) throughout.

screens.name: Chapter (expanded ring)
screens.description: Tap a chapter card's 'Read more' to open it as a full-height sheet: the full Wikipedia lead plus the History section, a swipeable photo strip from Commons (max 8), the facts strip expanded into a small timeline (inception, name changes, population points), a 'See on map' button that opens Big Map zoomed to that ring, and the sources list with licence text (CC BY-SA for Wikipedia, ODbL for OSM). Back arrow or swipe down returns to the same scroll position.

screens.name: Big Map
screens.description: Full-screen MapLibre map opened from the postcard or 'See on map'. Shows the pin, the current ring's outline (OSM admin boundary when available), and the basemap appropriate to the chosen date (see map_time_travel). The Time Dial stays available at the bottom so you can watch the map change. A top bar carries the date and a close button. Ring chips across the top (House, Street, City, Country...) re-zoom the map. At deep-time dates this screen becomes the Globe instead of a street map.

screens.name: Time Dial (bottom sheet)
screens.description: Collapsed (96px): the current date in large type ('1890', '1000 BCE', '66 million years ago - end of the Cretaceous'), a '<' and '>' stepper that moves one stop in the current gear, and a small 'Now' reset. Tap or drag up to expand (260px): a horizontally scrollable gear chip row (Years, Decades, Centuries, Millennia, Ice ages, Millions, Eons), a full-width snapping slider spanning only the selected gear's stops, and a 'Chapters' button that opens the named-stops list. Changing the date re-renders the story while keeping the scroll pinned to the ring you were reading.

screens.name: Chapters list
screens.description: A simple vertical list of named time stops (Now; Living memory 1975; Grandparents' time 1925; Boom years 1875; Early modern 1600; Medieval / pre-contact 1000; Antiquity 1 CE; Farming begins 8000 BCE; Ice age peak 20,000 years ago; First humans 300,000 years ago; Age of mammals 34 Ma; Last day of the dinosaurs 66 Ma; Age of dinosaurs 150 Ma; Pangaea 250 Ma; Coal forests 300 Ma; Life comes ashore 400 Ma; Cambrian seas 520 Ma; Snowball Earth 700 Ma; First continents 3 Ga; Birth of the Earth 4.5 Ga). Each row shows a one-line teaser specific to this address when we have the data ('Your city is 24 years old', 'Your spot is under a shallow sea at 12 degrees south'). Tapping a row sets the dial and closes the list.

screens.name: Globe (deep-time map)
screens.description: Replaces the map postcard and Big Map when the date is 1 million years ago or older. An orthographic globe drawn with d3-geo as inline SVG: reconstructed coastlines for the chosen stop, a glowing dot for where this address was then, a faint ghost outline of today's continents for orientation, and a caption with paleolatitude ('12 degrees S, near the equator'). Drag to rotate. Beyond the oldest plate model the globe shows no coastlines and the caption says so.

screens.name: About & Sources
screens.description: Plain page: what the site is, that it runs entirely in your browser, which services it talks to (OpenStreetMap/Nominatim, Wikipedia/Wikidata/Wikimedia Commons, OpenHistoricalMap, Macrostrat, Paleobiology Database, GPlates), that your typed address is sent to those services and nowhere else, licence notes, and a 'this is a hobby site; history can be wrong, tell us' line with the owner's contact or GitHub issues link.

concepts.time_scale_design:
Principle: the dial is a gearbox, not one slider. One continuous slider from 1 year to 4.5 billion years is unusable on a 340px-wide phone, so the user first picks a gear (how big a step), then scrubs a slider that spans only that gear, with a stepper for exact stops. Every position is a discrete, named stop; the dial always snaps. Internally the current time is a single object {kind:'year', value:1890} or {kind:'ago', value:66e6}; the URL encodes it as at=1890, at=-8000 (BCE), at=20ka, at=66Ma, at=2.5Ga, at=now.

Gears and exact stops (266 stops total):
1. YEARS: 2026 down to 1870, step 1 year (157 stops). Readout '1890'.
2. DECADES: 1860 down to 1500, step 10 (37 stops). Readout '1860s'.
3. CENTURIES: 1400, 1300, ..., 100, 1 CE, 100 BCE, 200 BCE, ..., 1000 BCE (25 stops). Readout '1300s' / '500 BCE'.
4. MILLENNIA: 2000 BCE, 3000 BCE, ..., 12,000 BCE (11 stops; 12,000 BCE is roughly the end of the last ice age). Readout '8000 BCE (about 10,000 years ago)'.
5. ICE AGES: 20,000; 30,000; 50,000; 75,000; 100,000; 150,000; 200,000; 300,000; 500,000; 750,000 years ago (10 stops). Readout '20,000 years ago - ice age peak'.
6. MILLIONS (geologic period boundaries, which is what the fossil and plate data are organised by): 1, 2.6 (Quaternary begins), 5.3 (Pliocene), 23 (Neogene), 34 (Oligocene), 56 (Eocene), 66 (end of the dinosaurs), 100, 145 (Cretaceous begins), 201 (Jurassic), 252 (Triassic / great dying), 299 (Permian), 359 (Carboniferous), 419 (Devonian), 444 (Silurian), 485 (Ordovician), 539 (Cambrian) million years ago (17 stops). Readout '66 million years ago - end of the Cretaceous'.
7. EONS: 635 (Ediacaran), 720 (Snowball Earth), 1000 (Rodinia), 1600, 2500 (Proterozoic begins), 3000, 3500 (earliest life), 4000 (Hadean), 4567 (Earth forms) million years ago (9 stops). Readout '2.5 billion years ago'.

Controls: gear chip row (horizontally scrollable, current gear highlighted, each chip shows its range in small text, e.g. 'Decades 1860-1500'); per-gear snapping slider with tick marks every 10th stop and a large live readout above the thumb; '<' '>' stepper buttons (44px targets) moving one stop; long-press on a stepper auto-repeats at 4 stops/second. Rolling over: if the slider is dragged into the end-stop of a gear and held for 300ms, the dial shifts to the neighbouring gear with a short vibration (navigator.vibrate(10)) and the readout shows 'Switching to centuries'. Keyboard: Left/Right step, Shift+Left/Right change gear, Home = Now. 'Chapters' button opens the named-stops list (20 named stops drawn from across the gears) so people who do not care about gears can still jump to the famous moments. A 'Now' reset is always visible.

Story coupling: changing the date never resets scroll position; the page re-renders chapters in place and keeps the ring you were reading at the top, so you can sit on 'City' and flip 1890 -> 1850 -> 1800 like turning editions of the same book. When the date crosses the age of the bedrock under the house (from Macrostrat), the dial readout flashes 'The rock under your house is forming right now' and the Rock chapter is highlighted; this is a deliberate wow moment that costs nothing. When the date crosses 1 million years ago in either direction, the postcard animates a zoom-out from the street map to the Globe (or back), signalling the change in what 'map' means.
concepts.rings_design:
Rings are the chapters of the scroll, always in the same order small to big: 1 House/lot, 2 Block, 3 Street, 4 Neighborhood, 5 City/town, 6 County/region, 7 State/province, 8 Country, 9 Continent, then the Deep Time chapters (The land, The rock under your house, Where this spot was, Life here then). Each chapter card has: eyebrow 'RING 5 - YOUR CITY: Portland', title, a 'then' facts strip (founded / population at this date / name at this date / country at this date, only showing items we actually have), 1-4 paragraphs, an optional photo, a mini-map thumbnail is NOT rendered per card (one shared postcard zooms instead), 'Read more' and source chips.

Navigation: (a) the tree-ring glyph in the sticky header: nine concentric circles; the ring you are currently reading is filled; ring thickness is proportional to how much we found (paragraph count), so a rich city and a thin house literally look like a wide ring and a hairline, which makes the data reality part of the metaphor instead of a failure. Tap the glyph to open a ring picker (vertical list with thickness bars) and jump. (b) IntersectionObserver marks the current ring as cards pass the top of the viewport and drives both the glyph and the postcard zoom (house z18, block z17, street z16, neighborhood z14, city z11, county z9, state z6, country z4, continent z2, deep time = globe). (c) Swipe-up on the End card goes back to the top.

Empty and thin rings: a ring is never removed in the present day; it becomes a 'thin ring' card (half height, dashed left rule, muted) that still says something true, then points outward. Concrete empty states: HOUSE with no article: 'No written history found for this exact house - that's normal, almost no houses have one. Here's what the map knows:' then OSM building tags (type, floors, year built if start_date exists, historic tags) and 'The street has more below'. If even the footprint is missing: 'The map doesn't have this building drawn yet. Lot location only.' BLOCK with no article: list the oldest named things within 120m from OSM ('Elders of the block: St Mary's church (1887), the corner shop, Lincoln Park') or, if none, 'A quiet block: nothing named within a minute's walk on the map.' STREET with no article: show 'named after' from the OSM name:etymology:wikidata tag when present ('Maple Street is named after... the tree, apparently'), otherwise 'We couldn't find who or what this street is named after.' NEIGHBORHOOD missing from the geocode: skip the ring entirely in the present (the glyph shows 8 rings) and say in the Hero's summary line 'No neighborhood on record for this address'. COUNTY/STATE missing (countries without those levels): skip silently; rings are whatever the admin hierarchy actually returns, so a Paris address gets arrondissement -> Paris -> Ile-de-France -> France.

Rings over time: each ring has an existence state at the chosen date: exists / not-yet / unknown / folded. 'Not yet' uses the Wikidata inception date (P571) for city, county, state, country and OSM start_date for the building; the card becomes a 'Not yet' card: 'Not yet. Portland will be founded in 1851 - 61 years from this date. The land is part of ...' (the next ring up that does exist). When the building year is unknown, the house and block rings inherit the city's founding as a hedge and say 'Probably not yet - we don't know when this house was built, but the city wasn't founded until 1851.' Country changes (a city that was Spanish, then Mexican, then American) come from Wikidata P17 with date qualifiers and show in the facts strip. From 20,000 years ago and older, all human rings fold into one chapter, 'The land', and the scroll shortens to: The land -> The rock under your house -> Where this spot was -> Life here then -> Earth. The glyph draws folded rings dotted so the reader sees the rings 'closing' as they go back in time.
concepts.map_time_travel:
The map is a single MapLibre instance in the sticky postcard (lazy-loaded on first interaction or after the story renders, whichever is first), swapped for the SVG Globe at 1 million years and older. What it shows per gear:

YEARS and DECADES (2026-1500): OpenHistoricalMap vector tiles with the style's date filter set to the chosen stop, so buildings, roads and names that existed then appear and later ones vanish. After each date change the page counts rendered OHM features in the viewport; if the count is below a threshold (roughly 'fewer than 10 features at the city zoom'), we switch to the fallback: today's OpenStreetMap basemap rendered in sepia/greyscale with roads and buildings faded to 30%, water and coastline kept, and a small persistent label on the postcard: 'No historical map for this area in 1890 - showing today's streets, faded.' Any OHM features that do exist are drawn on top at full strength, so a single 1890 railway line still shows. The pin is always drawn. Hero text also states the fallback once so the reader is never misled.

CENTURIES (1400-1000 BCE): OHM is mostly empty here except for some historical borders and ancient cities. Base layer becomes the bundled 'nature-only' map: Natural Earth coastlines, rivers, lakes and a hillshade raster from OHM/OSM where available, with NO political lines or roads. OHM historical boundaries and settlements for the date are drawn on top if present. Label: 'Land and water as today; borders and towns only where recorded.'

MILLENNIA and ICE AGES (12,000 BCE - 750,000 years ago): same nature-only base. Caption adds 'Coastlines shown are today's; sea level was lower during ice ages.' If a permissively licensed last-glacial-maximum ice-sheet polygon can be bundled it is drawn as a translucent white layer at the 20,000-year stop; otherwise the ice age is told in text only. No OHM here.

MILLIONS (1-539 Ma): the postcard animates a zoom-out to the Globe. The Globe draws reconstructed coastlines for the stop (precomputed GeoJSON bundled in the repo for all 17 stops so the map never depends on a live service), a ghost of modern continents, and the address's reconstructed position fetched live from the GPlates web service for the exact stop ('Your spot was here, at 12 degrees S'). If the live point fetch fails: globe without the dot and the caption 'Couldn't place your spot for this era right now - try again.'

EONS (635 Ma - 4.5 Ga): the Globe shows reconstructed coastlines only as far back as the bundled model goes (about 1 billion years); beyond that it shows a plain globe with no land and the caption 'No reliable map of the continents this far back.' At 4 Ga and 4.5 Ga the globe is drawn as a CSS-gradient molten orb with 'No oceans yet' / 'The Earth is forming'. Nothing pretends to be data.

Everywhere: the postcard carries a one-line map caption so the reader always knows whether they are looking at a historical map, a faded modern map, or a reconstruction. Big Map is the same instance expanded; the Time Dial stays available there so people can watch streets appear and vanish.
concepts.data_to_ui_mapping:
Front-end architecture: a static Vite + vanilla TypeScript (or Preact) site deployed by GitHub Actions to GitHub Pages; hash routing (#/story?q=&at=) so refresh and share work without server config. Modules: geocode.ts (Nominatim), hierarchy.ts (Wikidata P131 chain), wiki.ts (Wikipedia REST + Commons), osm.ts (building and nearby features), deeptime.ts (Macrostrat, PBDB, GPlates), timeline.ts (gears/stops/encode-decode), story.ts (builds Chapter objects for a date), render/ (Hero, ChapterCard, RingGlyph, Postcard, Globe, TimeDial). Every fetch goes through one cached fetch helper (sessionStorage + in-memory, keyed by URL) that sets the Api-User-Agent header for Wikimedia and spaces Nominatim calls at least 1 second apart. A Chapter is {ring, exists:'yes'|'notyet'|'unknown'|'folded', title, factsThen[], paragraphs[], image?, sources[], richness:number}.

Address -> rings: Nominatim /search?format=jsonv2&addressdetails=1&extratags=1&namedetails=1 gives lat/lon, osm_type/osm_id, and address parts (house_number, road, neighbourhood/suburb, city/town/village, county, state, country) plus wikidata/wikipedia extratags when tagged. The city's Wikidata QID (from extratags, or a Wikidata search on 'city, state') seeds a P131 'located in' walk upward to the country and P30 for the continent; each hop becomes a ring with a QID. Nominatim's 1-request-per-second rule drives the no-autocomplete decision and the 'Go' button.

Per ring -> card: Wikidata entity gives inception (P571) -> 'Founded' fact and the not-yet rule; population with point-in-time qualifiers (P1082) -> 'Population then' fact (nearest point at or before the date); official name with dates (P1448) -> 'Then called'; country with dates (P17) -> 'Then part of'; image (P18) -> photo; sitelinks -> Wikipedia title. Wikipedia REST /page/summary/{title} gives the lead paragraph and thumbnail for the present-day card; the action API (prop=extracts&section=History, origin=*) gives the History section for the expanded Chapter view. For past dates in MVP+1, a 'chapter finder' heuristic splits the History text into paragraphs, tags each with the four-digit years it mentions, and shows the paragraphs whose years fall at or just before the chosen date, labelled 'From the Wikipedia article, paragraphs that mention years around 1890'.

House: the Nominatim result's osm_id, fetched via Overpass or the OSM API (/api/0.6/way/{id}) for building, building:levels, start_date, historic, heritage tags and the footprint polygon -> thin ring facts and the pin outline. Block: one Overpass query around:120m for named features with tags (amenity, shop, leisure, historic, building with start_date) -> 'Elders of the block' list sorted by start_date. Street: the road way's name:etymology:wikidata tag -> Wikidata label and description -> 'Named after'; a Wikipedia search for '"<road>" <city>' -> street article if one exists (common for famous streets, rare otherwise). Neighborhood: Wikipedia search for '<neighbourhood>, <city>'.

Deep time: Macrostrat /api/v2/geologic_units/map?lat=&lng= -> unit name, lithology, b_age/t_age, description -> 'The rock under your house' card and the 'rock forming now' dial callout; /api/v2/defs/intervals supplies the standard geologic period names and colours used for gear 6 and 7 chips. PBDB /data1.2/occs/list with a 50km box and interval filter -> 'Life here then' card listing up to 8 fossil taxa found nearby from that period, with 'nearest find 32 km away'. GPlates web service reconstruct_points at the chosen stop -> paleo lat/lon dot on the Globe; bundled precomputed coastline GeoJSON per stop -> globe land. Natural Earth (public domain) bundled -> nature-only basemap for pre-map eras.

Attribution: every card lists its sources; the footer carries the mandatory OSM, OHM, Wikipedia (CC BY-SA) and Macrostrat/PBDB credits. Text from Wikipedia is quoted, not rewritten, to stay inside the licence.
concepts.mobile: Designed phone-first (most visits). Layout: single column, 16px gutters, cards full width, 17px body type with 1.5 line height, system font stack (no web font download). Sticky header 56px; postcard map 180px sticky under it, collapsing to 96px once the reader scrolls past the Hero so the story owns the screen; the Time Dial is a bottom sheet at 96px collapsed, 260px expanded, inside the thumb zone with 44px targets. The map uses cooperativeGestures so one-finger scrolling never gets trapped in the map; two fingers or tapping into Big Map pans it. One map instance only; chapters never embed their own maps. Images: one per card, lazy-loaded, Commons thumbnails requested at 640px width, with width/height set to avoid layout shift. Fetching is progressive: geocode and hierarchy first (Hero appears within about 2 seconds), then each ring's Wikipedia summary as its card scrolls near the viewport (IntersectionObserver with a 600px margin), deep-time calls last. Skeleton cards keep the ring order visible while loading. MapLibre (about 800KB) loads only after the first chapter renders, and not at all if the reader never scrolls past the Hero on a slow connection (Save-Data header respected). Date changes re-render cards in place without scroll jumps. Share: Web Share API with the address and date in the URL, fallback copy-to-clipboard. Desktop gets a two-column layout: story 60% left, map sticky right, Time Dial as a right-side rail; everything else identical. Accessibility: cards are articles with headings, the glyph and dial are keyboard operable, readouts are aria-live, prefers-reduced-motion disables the zoom-out and globe animations.
concepts.mvp_cut:
MVP ('delightful in one afternoon of reading'): Front Door with Nominatim geocode, disambiguation list and example chips; The Story scroll with the Hero one-sentence biography; rings House (thin ring from OSM building tags), Street ('named after' from the OSM etymology tag plus a Wikipedia search), Neighborhood (best-effort Wikipedia search, skipped if nothing), City, State/Province, Country, Continent (all via the Wikidata P131 chain + Wikipedia summary + one photo + inception/population facts); Deep Time chapters 'The rock under your house' (Macrostrat) and 'Where this spot was' (Globe with bundled coastlines at a handful of stops and the live GPlates dot); the tree-ring glyph with thickness-by-richness and tap-to-jump; the sticky postcard map with per-ring zoom, OHM date filtering, and the faded-modern-map fallback with its caption; the Time Dial in Chapters-only mode (the 20 named stops in the Chapters list, plus the '<' '>' stepper moving between them; no gears, no slider yet); the 'Not yet' rule from inception dates and the folded Deep Time scroll; the 'rock forming now' callout; share URL; About & Sources. That set already delivers the three wow moments: the one-sentence biography, the countdown 'your city will be founded in 61 years', and the glowing dot on a 250-million-year-old globe.

Defer to MVP+1: the full gearbox (7 gears, 266 stops, slider, rollover, keyboard); Block ring and 'Elders of the block' (needs Overpass and tuning); County ring; 'Life here then' fossils from PBDB; the chapter-finder heuristic for Wikipedia history paragraphs at past dates; name-then / country-then facts over time; the expanded Chapter sheet with photo strips; the ice-sheet overlay; autoplay 'play through time'; offline caching. Never (for this product): user accounts, user-submitted edits, server-side rendering, paid geocoders, generated social-preview images (use one static preview image).
concepts.risks: 1. Nominatim policy: it forbids autocomplete and heavy use, and an unattributed or bursty hobby site can be blocked by IP; mitigations are no autocomplete, submit-only search, 1 req/sec spacing, caching, prominent attribution, and a clear 'the address service is busy, try again in a minute' error state. 2. Thin house and block rings disappoint if presented as failures; the thin-ring treatment, honest copy, and the strong Hero sentence are what make the product feel complete rather than broken, and should not be cut. 3. OpenHistoricalMap coverage is patchy, so the faded-modern-map fallback and its caption must be unmistakable, or readers will believe 1890 streets looked like today's. 4. Wikipedia text is about a whole city, not a date; the past-date 'chapter finder' is a heuristic and must be labelled as such, which is why it is deferred and why MVP only uses dated Wikidata facts for past stops. 5. Deep-time services (GPlates, Macrostrat, PBDB) are small academic APIs that can be slow or down; bundling the globe coastlines and showing the globe without the dot on failure keeps the chapter usable. 6. Page weight on phones: MapLibre plus photos can exceed 2MB; lazy-loading the map, one image per card and Save-Data handling are required, not optional. 7. Licensing: Wikipedia text is CC BY-SA (quote, attribute, link), OSM/OHM are ODbL (attribute), Commons images carry per-file licences (show the credit on the expanded view); the About page and card source chips carry these. 8. Sensitivity: pre-colonial chapters must not read as 'empty land'; the 'Medieval / pre-contact' and 'First people' stops should show the region's recorded Indigenous history from Wikipedia where it exists and say 'we have no recorded history for this exact spot' where it does not, never inventing specifics. 9. Geocoding ambiguity and rural addresses: show the disambiguation list and degrade to lot-only rings without errors. 10. Privacy: typed addresses are sent to third-party APIs; state it plainly on the About page and run no analytics. 11. Accuracy of 'not yet' countdowns depends on Wikidata inception dates, which are sometimes missing or approximate; show 'about' when the date has year precision only and 'unknown' rather than guessing. 12. Owner is a beginner: keep the architecture to plain modules, one build command and one GitHub Action, and write the data adapters so each ring can fail independently without breaking the scroll.

concepts.angle: MAP-FIRST. The map fills the screen edge to edge and is the only "page". The time control (a draggable ruler we call the Time Tape) is the hero and lives across the bottom of every view. The nine rings (house -> plate) are not pages or tabs: they are map zoom levels with a snap-to "ring ladder", and the map draws the current ring's boundary around the pin. Text is a reactive side panel (bottom sheet on phones, right column on laptops) whose contents are a pure function of two things: which ring you are looking at and where the Time Tape sits. Nothing is ever blank: when a ring or a time has no written history, the map still has something honest to show and the panel says what it does and does not know.
concepts.concept:
You type an address (or just tap anywhere on the map) and the map flies down to that house. The whole screen is map. The only other things on it are a short ladder of rings on the right edge and a big ruler of time across the bottom. The rings are simply zoom levels: House, Street, Neighborhood, City, County, State, Country, and finally the Plate the whole continent rides on. Tap a ring and the map glides out to that level and draws a soft glowing outline of that ring around your house. A panel slides up from the bottom (or sits beside the map on a laptop) and tells the story of whatever ring you are looking at, right now, at the moment in time you have chosen.

The time ruler is the star. It works like a tape measure you drag under a fixed needle. Drag it and the map changes under your thumb: today's streets fade to a faint ghost, old roads and buildings appear wherever the historical map has them, your own house disappears in the year it was built, and the city's border turns to a dashed line before the city existed. Pinch the tape (or tap the little magnifier buttons) and the ruler changes units: years, then decades, centuries, thousands of years, millions of years, and finally the named chapters of Earth's history (Jurassic, Cretaceous, and so on). A few thousand years back the map lifts off into a globe and your house rides its continent across the planet, while the panel tells you what rock is under the floor, how old it is, and what the world was like.

Honesty is part of the design. For most houses nobody has written anything about the house itself, so the panel never pretends. It shows the facts it has (what kind of building, how many floors, when it was built if anyone recorded it), then the nearest stories and photos, and tells you how far away they are. Little filled or hollow dots on the ring ladder and on the time ruler show at a glance which rings and which periods actually have something to read, so friends naturally drift toward the rich parts (the city in 1900, the continent 200 million years ago) instead of hitting dead ends.

The whole site is a folder of files on GitHub Pages: no server, no accounts, no keys, nothing to pay for. Everything is fetched live, inside the visitor's phone, from free public sources (OpenStreetMap for addresses and borders, Wikipedia and Wikimedia Commons for stories and photos, OpenHistoricalMap for old maps, Macrostrat for the rock underfoot, GPlates for where the continents were). Every view has its own link, so "my house in 1924" or "my street in the Cretaceous" can be texted to a friend and they land exactly there.

screens.name: Start (map + search)
screens.description: Full-bleed world map (or the visitor's country if the browser's locale hints it), dimmed 30%, with one centered search box: placeholder 'Type an address or tap the map'. Controls: text field + Go button (search fires on Enter/Go, never per keystroke, to respect Nominatim's no-autocomplete rule), 'Use my location' button (optional, browser geolocation, nothing stored), three example chips (owner's own picks, e.g. a famous address in their city). Tapping the dimmed map drops a pin and skips the address step entirely, which is the fallback for places without addresses. Empty/error states: no results -> 'Couldn't find that. Add a city or country, or tap the map to drop a pin.'; several results -> a 5-row list with the matched address text and a tiny map thumbnail; geolocation denied -> silently hide the button. First visit also shows 3 coach marks after the first fly-in: 'Drag the tape to travel in time', 'Pinch the tape to change units', 'Tap a ring to zoom out'.

screens.name: Place (the main screen)
screens.description: Map fills the screen. Fixed chrome: (1) top-left address chip showing the resolved short address, tap to change; (2) top-right 'Here' (recenter on pin) and 'Now' (jump to today) buttons; (3) right-edge Ring Ladder (see rings_design); (4) bottom Time Tape with its rung pill, step buttons and overview strip (see time_scale_design); (5) the Story Sheet docked above the tape in 'peek' state (one line: ring name, the time, a headline, the data dots). The pin is a small house glyph that is always kept inside the visible map area (map padding accounts for the sheet and tape). The current ring boundary is drawn as a glowing outline; the house footprint is drawn solid at House/Street rings. Map state (pin, ring, time, rung) is written to the URL hash so every view is a link.

screens.name: Story Sheet (the reactive panel)
screens.description: Bottom sheet with three detents on phones (peek 64px, half 46% of height, full); a fixed 400px right column on laptops. Its content is computed from (ring, time) and is a stack of independent cards, each with its own loading, empty and error state so one dead source never blanks the panel. Card order for historical time: Header ('Brooklyn in 1924', or 'Brooklyn: not yet founded (1834)'), Facts (population at that time, country it belonged to, official name then, inception), Moments (sentences from the ring's Wikipedia article that mention years within the current step, nearest first, each with a 'read on Wikipedia' link), Photos (Commons photos taken nearest to the chosen year within the ring's radius, with distance and date), Nearest stories (for thin rings: Wikipedia places within the ring, sorted by distance), Sources (attribution lines). Card order for deep time: Header ('The ground under 12 Main St, 180 million years ago · Jurassic'), Where was here (paleolatitude, hemisphere, which continent/plate, a 40px mini globe), Rock under the house (Macrostrat unit name, age range, rock type, one-line description, 'forming right now' badge if its age range includes the chosen time), This chapter of Earth (hand-written 2-3 sentence blurb per period from a static JSON shipped with the site), Fossils found nearby (v2), Sources. Empty states are written as sentences, never as a grey box: 'No one has written about this street on Wikipedia yet. Nearest story: Prospect Park (600 m).'

screens.name: Ring Ladder (expanded)
screens.description: On phones the ladder is a single pill at the right edge showing the current ring name with up/down chevrons; tapping it expands a vertical ladder of 7-9 notches (House, Block, Street, Neighborhood, City, County, State, Country, Plate) with the ring's actual name under each ('Street: Dean St', 'City: New York'). Each notch has a dot: filled = has a story or photos at the current time, hollow = nothing written, dashed = ring didn't exist yet at this time. Tap a notch to fly there; swipe up/down on the pill to step rings. Notches for rings that do not exist for this address (no neighborhood, no state) are omitted, so the ladder is shorter rather than lying.

screens.name: Jump to time sheet
screens.description: Opened by tapping the Time Tape's readout. Two parts: a text field that accepts '1924', '1850s', '3000 BCE', '20k', '66M', '4.5B'; and a scrollable list of named stops (every rung's named marks and all 15 Earth chapters, each with a colored swatch and 'what happened' one-liner). Picking one sets both the time and the appropriate rung.

screens.name: Photo viewer
screens.description: Full-screen lightbox for a Commons photo: image, date taken, distance from the pin, author and license line (required by Commons licenses), 'Open on Commons' link, swipe left/right to move through photos ordered by date. A 'Show on map' button drops a camera glyph where the photo was taken.

screens.name: Share sheet
screens.description: Native share (Web Share API) on phones, copy-link on desktop. The link encodes lat/lon, ring, rung and time, e.g. #/40.6782,-73.9442/city/yr/1924. A preview line reads back what the link opens: 'Brooklyn in 1924'. v2: a generated PNG card (map snapshot + headline) via a canvas capture.

screens.name: About and sources
screens.description: Static page reachable from the address chip menu. Explains what the site is, what it does with the address (sent to OpenStreetMap's Nominatim and Wikipedia-family services to look things up; nothing stored by this site; no analytics), and the attribution block required by each source: OpenStreetMap contributors (ODbL), OpenHistoricalMap (CC0), Wikipedia text (CC BY-SA, linked per card), Wikimedia Commons (per-photo credit), Macrostrat (CC BY), GPlates Web Service and the reconstruction model used (model license named), PBDB (CC BY) when fossils ship.

concepts.time_scale_design:
THE CONTROL: a Time Tape across the bottom of the screen. It is a ruler that scrolls horizontally under a fixed center needle; older is to the left, so you drag the tape to the right to go back in time. Momentum fling, snap to the nearest step on release, a soft haptic tick (navigator.vibrate(5)) on each snap where supported. Tape height 88px; step pitch 28px on phones (so about 14 steps are visible on a 390px phone), 36px on laptops. Above the tape sits a rung pill (segmented control: YR · 10YR · 100YR · 1K · 1M · CHAPTERS) and two magnifier buttons (+ zooms time in to a finer rung, - zooms out); pinching the tape does the same. Left and right of the tape are 44px step buttons that move exactly one step at the current rung; holding them repeats. The needle shows the readout in 20px type with a one-line context label beneath it. Tapping the readout opens the Jump sheet. A thin 4px Overview Strip runs the full width above the rung pill: a log scale of 'years ago' from 1 year (right) to 4.54 billion (left), shaded in six bands for the six rungs, with a marker for the current time and small dots wherever the current ring has content (sentence years, photo dates, map features, rock ages). Tapping the strip jumps there and sets the rung automatically. Keyboard on laptops: Left/Right step, Shift+Left/Right 10 steps, [ and ] change rung, N = Now.

THE SIX RUNGS (exact steps, ranges, labels, readout):
1. YEARS: step 1 year. Range: 1700 CE to today. Ticks every year, labels every 10 years. Readout '1924' with sub-label '102 years ago'. Default position on load: today. Dragging past 1700 shows an end cap 'Earlier: switch to decades' (tap to switch); nothing auto-switches while a finger is down.
2. DECADES: step 10 years. Range: 1 CE to today (no year zero; display '1 CE'). Labels every 100 years. Readout '1920s' with sub-label '106 years ago'. For map filtering and data lookups, a decade means its first year.
3. CENTURIES: step 100 years. Range: 10,000 BCE to today. Labels every 1,000 years. Readout '1800s' for CE and '3000 BCE' for BCE. Named marks drawn as small flags on the tape, from a static JSON shipped with the site: first farming ~9500 BCE, first cities ~3500 BCE, writing ~3200 BCE, bronze ~3000 BCE, iron ~1200 BCE, 1 CE.
4. MILLENNIA: step 1,000 years. Range: 10,000 years ago to 300,000 years ago. Labels every 10,000. Readout '18,000 years ago' with sub-label from a static climate table ('Last Ice Age peak'). Named marks: 11,700 (Holocene begins, ice retreats), 15,000 (people reach the Americas), 20,000 (ice age peak, sea 120 m lower), 45,000 (people in Europe and Australia), 70,000 (people leave Africa), 300,000 (earliest Homo sapiens). The band 300,000 to 1,000,000 years ago is deliberately unreachable: no source we use changes across it, and the tape's end cap says so ('Nothing on our maps changes until 1 million years ago: switch to millions').
5. MILLIONS: step 1 million years. Range: 1 Ma to 1,000 Ma (the limit of the plate model). Ticks every 1 Myr, labels every 10 Myr, and a colored band under the tape with the geologic period names (standard ICS colors, served by Macrostrat's intervals endpoint or baked into a static JSON). Readout '180 million years ago' with sub-label 'Jurassic'. End cap beyond 1,000 Ma: 'Before 1 billion years ago: chapters only'.
6. CHAPTERS (eons/eras/periods): not a ruler but a row of 15 equal-width chips (96px each) on the same tape, so the same drag gesture works. Stops, each with the time the map actually renders in parentheses: Hadean 4,540-4,000 Ma (map: stylized globe, no continents); Archean 4,000-2,500 Ma (stylized); Proterozoic 2,500-539 Ma (map at 750 Ma, the oldest the model covers, labeled 'shown: 750 Ma'); Cambrian 539-485 (510); Ordovician 485-444 (465); Silurian 444-419 (430); Devonian 419-359 (390); Carboniferous 359-299 (330); Permian 299-252 (275); Triassic 252-201 (230); Jurassic 201-145 (170); Cretaceous 145-66 (100); Paleogene 66-23 (45); Neogene 23-2.6 (12); Quaternary 2.6 Ma-now (map at 20,000 years ago). Readout: 'Jurassic · 201-145 million years ago'. Step buttons move chapter to chapter.

RUNG CHANGES KEEP YOUR PLACE: zooming out from 1924 at YEARS lands on 1920s at DECADES, then 1900s at CENTURIES; zooming in from 'Jurassic' lands on 170 Ma at MILLIONS. Values outside a rung's range clamp to the nearest end. 'Now' always returns to today at YEARS. The tape, overview strip and readout are one component with one state: {rung, time} where time is stored internally as a signed float of years-before-present so every data source gets the same number.
concepts.rings_design:
RINGS ARE ZOOM LEVELS. Each ring is bound to a map zoom and a camera rule, and the map always draws the current ring's boundary as a glowing outline around the pin: House = zoom 18.5, pin centered, building footprint filled; Block = zoom 17, a polygon bounded by the surrounding streets (v2) or, until then, omitted from the ladder; Street = zoom 16, the named road's line highlighted along its length (v2) or a 300 m circle (MVP); Neighborhood = zoom 14.5, boundary polygon if OSM has one, else a 1 km circle labeled 'approx.'; City/town = fit the city boundary, min zoom 11; County/region = fit boundary; State/province = fit boundary; Country = fit boundary, max zoom 5; Plate = zoom 1.5 in globe projection, the tectonic plate polygon containing the pin highlighted. Rings whose entity does not exist for this address (no neighborhood, no county, no state in a small country) are dropped from the ladder, and two adjacent rings that resolve to the same entity (a city that is also its county) are merged into one notch labeled 'City · County'. So a ladder has between 6 and 9 notches and never shows a fake level.

NAVIGATION: the Ring Ladder on the right edge. On phones it is a 40px pill at mid-height showing the current ring's name; tap to expand the vertical ladder, swipe up/down on the pill to step one ring. On laptops the full ladder is always visible. Pinch-zooming the map also moves the ladder: at gesture end the map snaps to the nearest ring ('magnetic rings', snapping disabled while a finger is down so free exploration still works). Keyboard 1-9 jumps to a ring. The ladder's icon is the brand mark: nine concentric circles with the current one filled. Each notch carries a status dot recomputed whenever time changes: filled = this ring has a story or photos at this time; hollow = nothing written; dashed = this entity did not exist yet at this time (inception from Wikidata is later than the chosen time); grey = still loading. The dots are the honesty mechanism: in 1850 the House and Street dots are usually hollow and City is filled, so people see where to go.

WHAT THE PANEL SHOWS PER RING (today / historical): House: OSM facts (building type, levels, name, heritage listing, start_date if present, else 'Built: unknown'), Wikidata items within 100 m (listed buildings often have photos and inception dates), Commons photos within 60 m. Street: the road's OSM name and type, Wikipedia geosearch within 300 m, photos within 300 m, Wikidata named-after (P138) if the street has an item. Neighborhood: Wikipedia summary + year-mined Moments + photos within the boundary. City, County, State, Country: the rich rings; summary, Moments near the chosen time, population at the chosen time, country-at-the-time, historical names, photos nearest in date. Plate: plate name, paleolatitude, rock under the house, chapter blurb. In deep time (MILLIONS and CHAPTERS) every ring from House to Country shows the same geology-centric cards but keeps its geographic frame ('the ground under 12 Main St', 'the land that will be Ohio'), and the admin boundary is drawn dashed and labeled 'today's border'.

WHEN A RING HAS NO DATA: the map still renders (every ring has a map, that is the point of map-first), the ring boundary still draws, and the panel shows, in order: (1) the structured facts it does have from OSM/Nominatim, (2) one honest sentence ('No one has written about this block on Wikipedia yet.'), (3) a Nearest Stories card: Wikipedia places sorted by distance with meters shown, each tappable to fly the map there, (4) a Zoom Out card: 'Neighborhood: 3 stories, 12 photos' that moves up one ring. The photo card degrades the same way: 'No photos within 60 m. Closest: 1954, 220 m' and shows that one. If every ring is empty (remote places), the Country ring still has a Wikipedia article in practice, and the deep-time cards always have Macrostrat or the chapter blurb, so the ladder always has at least one filled dot.
concepts.map_time_travel:
THE RULE: the map is composited from layers whose visibility and opacity are driven by the chosen time, and a small Map Note chip at the bottom-left of the map always says in plain words what you are looking at, so a sparse map is never mistaken for 'nothing was here'.

TODAY (time = this year): present-day vector tiles (OpenFreeMap or OHM's own base, no key) in full color, OSM buildings, labels, the pin, the ring boundary.

HISTORICAL (YEARS, DECADES, CENTURIES rungs, 10,000 BCE to today): two layers. (a) OpenHistoricalMap vector tiles with the standard OHM date filter applied to every layer (features whose start/end decimal dates bracket the chosen time), drawn in full color: roads, buildings, rail, boundaries, place labels as they were. (b) A 'ghost' of today's base map underneath, desaturated, with opacity that fades as you go back: 0.55 at 1950, 0.4 at 1900, 0.25 at 1800, 0.12 at 1000 CE, 0 at 10,000 BCE. Where OHM is rich (some cities), the past map simply replaces the ghost; where OHM is empty, the ghost keeps the viewer oriented and the Map Note says 'No historical map for 1850 here yet; today's streets shown faded'. Your own house: if the building has a known start date (OSM start_date, OHM start date, or Wikidata inception for listed buildings) the footprint vanishes when the time is earlier than that, with a 'Not built yet' label at the pin; if the date is unknown the footprint is drawn dashed with 'Built: unknown'. Ring boundaries: drawn solid when the entity existed at that time (Wikidata inception <= time, or an OHM boundary with dates), dashed with the label 'border as of today' otherwise. Place labels from OHM carry old names automatically; on top of that the panel header uses Wikidata historical names when available. Photos: at Neighborhood and closer, camera glyphs mark where dated Commons photos were taken within +/- one step of the chosen time; tapping opens the viewer.

PREHISTORIC (MILLENNIA rung, 10,000 to 300,000 years ago): the base switches to a 'wilderness' style: terrain and water only, no roads, buildings or labels, the pin and a dashed ring boundary labeled 'today's border'. The Map Note states 'No people here yet' or the humans-arrival line from the static per-continent table. v2: last-glacial-maximum ice sheet and lowered-sea-level coastlines as static GeoJSON overlays.

DEEP TIME (MILLIONS and CHAPTERS rungs): the map switches by ring. At Plate ring (and automatically whenever the user zooms out past Country in deep time) the map becomes a globe (MapLibre globe projection): reconstructed coastlines and plate polygons for the chosen time from the GPlates Web Service, the pin re-plotted at its reconstructed position, and a thin trail showing the path the house's point has taken from that time to today. Scrubbing the tape at MILLIONS requests the reconstruction for each snapped step (debounced 150 ms, every result cached), so the continents visibly drift. At House through Country rings in deep time the map stays flat and shows the geologic map (Macrostrat's public tile layer) with units that were forming at the chosen time (unit age range brackets the time) drawn in full color and everything else muted; the Map Note reads 'Rock being laid down here 300 million years ago' or, when no unit matches, 'Nothing that formed in this period survives under this house; the rock here is Devonian'. A pill offers 'See the continent drift' (sets the Plate ring) because that is the better view at this rung.

WHEN NO HISTORICAL MAP DATA EXISTS, by case: OHM empty for this place and time -> ghost base plus Map Note (above). OHM present but only partially (a few roads) -> both layers, no note, the viewer sees the mix. Beyond 1,000 Ma (Hadean, Archean, early Proterozoic) -> a stylized globe with no continents, a note 'No reliable map of the continents exists for this time', and the panel leans on the chapter blurb and the rock card. Macrostrat has no geologic map coverage for the pin (oceans, some countries) -> the flat deep-time view falls back to the wilderness style with the note 'No geologic map here; zoom out to the Plate'. GPlates unavailable or slow -> the globe shows today's coastlines greyed with 'Couldn't load the plate map, retry', never a blank sphere; the 15 chapter stops are also shipped as static simplified GeoJSON in the repo so the CHAPTERS rung never depends on the live service at all.

THE SIGNATURE MOMENTS to protect: the house footprint blinking out in its build year; the ghost streets fading as you cross 1900; the city border going dashed; the lift-off from a flat map to a globe when the rung crosses into millions; and the pin sliding across the globe as the continents move.
concepts.data_to_ui_mapping:
ARCHITECTURE (static, no build step so a beginner can edit files directly): index.html + /js ES modules + /data static JSON and GeoJSON + /css. MapLibre GL JS from a CDN (globe projection built in, no Cesium). One state object {pin, rings[], ringIndex, rung, time} held in a tiny store; the URL hash is both the source of truth on load and written on every change. Three layers of code: services/ (one module per source with fetch, retry, cache, rate limit), resolvers/ (pure functions: (ring, time) -> panel cards; (rung, time) -> map layer settings), ui/ (tape, ladder, sheet, map). Every card renders independently; a failed or empty source changes only its own card. Caching: Cache API keyed by full request URL with stale-while-revalidate; recent addresses in localStorage; nothing else stored. A single request queue enforces Nominatim's 1 request/second and runs other sources in parallel. Deep-time code (globe, GPlates, Macrostrat) is a separate module loaded only the first time the rung crosses into millions, keeping the first load small for phones.

UI ELEMENT <- SOURCE (how it is called, limits, license):
- Address box -> Nominatim /search (format=jsonv2, addressdetails=1, extratags=1, namedetails=1, polygon_geojson=1, limit=5). Called on Enter only, max 1/s, browser sends Referer automatically which satisfies the identification rule. Returns the house footprint (if the match is a building), the address parts for every ring name, and the Wikidata ID when tagged. ODbL attribution in the footer.
- Ring boundaries -> Nominatim /reverse at fixed zoom levels with polygon_geojson=1 (zoom 16 street, 14 neighborhood/suburb, 10 city, 8 county, 5 state, 3 country), queued at 1/s in order of distance from the current ring, so the first boundary appears within a second and the rest fill in; until then rings draw as labeled 'approx.' circles. Each reverse result carries extratags.wikidata which is the key that links the ring to Wikipedia and Commons. v2: Overpass for the street polyline and for the block polygon (polygonize surrounding highway ways in the browser).
- Panel: Summary and Moments -> Wikipedia REST page summary (title from the Wikidata sitelink) for the header; for Moments the article's extract (action API, prop=extracts, origin=*), mined in the browser for sentences containing a year (regex for 1000-2026 with word boundaries, '19th century', 'BC/BCE', avoiding comma-grouped numbers), indexed by year once per ring, then filtered to the current step (+/- step/2) and sorted by distance from the chosen time. That year index also feeds the Overview Strip dots and the ladder's filled/hollow dots. CC BY-SA, every sentence links to its article.
- Panel: Facts at time T -> Wikidata entity JSON (Special:EntityData/Q.json, CORS open) for inception (P571), population series (P1082 with point-in-time qualifiers, pick the nearest), country (P17 with start/end qualifiers), official and native names with dates, 'replaces/replaced by' for predecessor entities. Wikidata SPARQL (CORS open) only for the 'items within N meters' query used at House and Street rings.
- Panel: Nearest stories -> Wikipedia action API list=geosearch (gsradius per ring: 100 m house, 300 m street, 1 km neighborhood) with origin=*, returns titles, coordinates and distance; summaries fetched lazily for the top 5.
- Photos -> Commons action API generator=geosearch with gsnamespace=6 and imageinfo extmetadata (DateTimeOriginal, Artist, LicenseShortName, thumbnail at 640px). Sorted by distance from the chosen year; cards show date, distance, credit line. Thumbnails only; full file link opens Commons.
- Historical map -> OpenHistoricalMap public vector tiles with OHM's published MapLibre style; the app rewrites every layer's filter with the chosen decimal date. CC0. Ghost base -> OpenFreeMap vector tiles (free, keyless, public sites allowed) or OHM's base.
- Rock under the house -> Macrostrat geologic_units/map (lat, lng) for unit name, age range, lithology, description; Macrostrat defs/intervals for period names and ICS colors (also baked into /data so the tape colors never wait on the network); Macrostrat public carto tiles for the deep-time flat map. CC BY.
- Where was here -> GPlates Web Service reconstruct/points (lon, lat, time, model with 1,000 Ma coverage) for the pin's reconstructed position and paleolatitude; reconstruct/coastlines and static plate polygons for the globe at MILLIONS steps, cached per step; the 15 CHAPTERS stops are pre-fetched once by the owner and committed to /data as simplified GeoJSON (same source, attributed, model license named on the About page).
- Fossils nearby (v2) -> Paleobiology Database occs/list.json with a bounding box around the pin and min_ma/max_ma from the chosen step; CC BY.
- World context fallback -> /data/context.json, hand-written by the owner with help: ~40 rows keyed by time band and continent (climate, people, animals), plus the 15 chapter blurbs. This is what fills the panel when every live source is empty, so the panel can never be blank.
- Overview Strip dots and ladder dots -> derived locally from: sentence years per ring, photo dates per ring, OHM features currently rendered in the viewport (queryRenderedFeatures start/end dates), Macrostrat unit age ranges. No extra requests.
- URL hash -> #/lat,lon/ring/rung/time (time as a year for CE/BCE, or '18k', '180M', 'jurassic'); the Share sheet just copies it.
concepts.mobile:
Phone-first, portrait. Layout from top: safe-area inset; address chip (top-left, 36px, truncated to 'Dean St, Brooklyn'); Here/Now buttons (top-right, 36px round); map everywhere; Ring pill docked to the right edge at mid-height (40px, expands into the ladder on tap, collapses on outside tap); Story Sheet peek (64px) docked above the Time Tape; the Time Tape block at the very bottom (overview strip 4px + rung pill 28px + tape 88px + safe-area), total about 128px. The map's padding is set so the pin always stays in the visible map area above the sheet, even when the sheet is at half height.

Gesture ownership (the main risk on a phone, solved by regions): horizontal drags on the tape belong to the tape, vertical drags on the sheet handle belong to the sheet, everything else belongs to the map. Pinch on the tape changes rung; pinch on the map changes ring. The tape uses touch-action: pan-y so the browser never scrolls the page; the whole app is position: fixed with no page scroll. Targets are 44px minimum; the tape's step buttons sit at the tape's ends under the thumbs. Haptic tick on snap where supported, none on iOS (no API), so the needle also flashes.

Landscape phone: the tape stays at the bottom, the sheet becomes a right drawer (40% width), the ladder stays on the right edge. Tablet and laptop: sheet becomes a fixed 400px right column, the tape spans the map width, the full ladder is always visible on the right of the map, and keyboard shortcuts work.

Performance budget: first load under 400 KB before map tiles (MapLibre is most of it), deep-time module loaded on demand, photo thumbnails 640px max, at most 12 photos per card, globe only at Plate ring or deep time (never at street zoom), OHM and base tiles never both at full opacity, and tape scrubbing throttled so network calls fire only on snapped steps, not on every pixel. prefers-reduced-motion disables the fly-to and drift animations and replaces them with cuts. Low-signal behavior: each card shows a skeleton for up to 8 seconds then a one-line 'Couldn't reach Wikipedia, tap to retry'; previously cached views open instantly from the Cache API. Dark mode follows the system and uses a dark map style so the glowing ring outline reads in both.
concepts.mvp_cut:
THE SMALLEST VERSION THAT IS DELIGHTFUL: type an address (or tap the map), the map flies to the house, you drag the Time Tape and watch today's streets fade into a ghost while the panel's sentences and photos change year by year, then you pinch out to the Chapters and watch your house ride its continent across a globe while the panel tells you what rock is underfoot. That loop touches the three things that feel like magic (time scrubbing, ring zoom, deep time) and skips everything that needs polish to be worth it.

MVP INCLUDES: Start screen with Nominatim search, map-tap pin and 'use my location'. Rings: House, Street (300 m circle), Neighborhood, City, County, State, Country, Plate; Block omitted (needs Overpass polygonizing). Ring boundaries from Nominatim reverse with the 'approx. circle until loaded' behavior; the ladder with filled/hollow/dashed dots. Time Tape with four rungs: YEARS, DECADES, CENTURIES and CHAPTERS. Historical map = OHM date-filtered tiles over the fading ghost base, house footprint vanishing when a build date is known, dashed anachronistic borders. Panel cards: Header, Facts (inception, population nearest the year, country at the time), Moments (year-mined sentences), Photos nearest the year, Nearest stories, Sources, plus the deep-time Rock and Where-was-here cards and the hand-written chapter blurbs. Chapters globe from 15 static GeoJSON files shipped in the repo plus one live GPlates point call per stop (cached), so deep time works even if the live service is down. Share link via URL hash. About page with all attributions. Coach marks on first visit.

DEFER TO V2 (in this order): the MILLENNIA and MILLIONS rungs (continuous drift animation and ice-age overlays); Block ring and true street polylines via Overpass; Fossils nearby from PBDB; Wikidata items-within-N-meters at the House ring (SPARQL is slower and flakier than everything else); camera glyphs on the map for dated photos; share cards as images; era color tints; a 'then and now' swipe comparison; the overview strip's data dots (ship the strip as a plain position gauge first, add dots when the year index exists).

SUGGESTED BUILD ORDER FOR THE OWNER (each step is a working site): 1) map + address + pin + URL hash; 2) ring ladder with Nominatim boundaries; 3) Time Tape at YEARS/DECADES/CENTURIES with the ghost fade and OHM filter; 4) panel with Wikipedia summary, then Moments and photos; 5) Chapters rung with the static globe files and the Macrostrat rock card; 6) dots, empty states, About page, coach marks; 7) share and polish.
concepts.risks:
1. Nominatim usage policy: 1 request/second, no autocomplete, must identify the app. Mitigation: search on Enter only, a single client-side queue, cache every response, lazy-load ring boundaries, and keep an eye on it if the link goes viral; the fallback is swapping the search module for another keyless OSM geocoder (e.g. Photon) which is a one-file change by design.
2. Sparse OpenHistoricalMap coverage: most addresses outside a handful of well-mapped cities will show only the ghost base in the past. Mitigation: the ghost fade plus the Map Note make this honest, the panel carries the experience in those places, and the Chapters rung works everywhere. Expectation risk remains: say 'old maps where they exist' in the About page and the coach marks.
3. House and Street rings will usually be thin or empty. Mitigation: facts-first cards, nearest stories with distances, the ladder dots steering people outward, and the world-context fallback. Accept that the delight is mostly at Neighborhood and above and in deep time; design the first fly-in to end at the House ring but with the City ring's headline already visible in the sheet peek so there is something to read immediately.
4. Year-mining Wikipedia sentences will sometimes produce irrelevant or misleading lines ('In 1924 the team won...' for a country ring, or population figures misread as years). Mitigation: strict regex (word boundaries, 1000-2026, not inside comma-grouped numbers), prefer the article's History section when the extract has headings, show the sentence verbatim with its link, label the card 'Mentions of 1924 on Wikipedia' rather than 'What happened', and cap it at five lines.
5. Volunteer-run services (OHM tiles, GPlates Web Service, Macrostrat, Overpass) can be slow, rate-limited, change their URLs or go down. Mitigation: every source behind one module with a timeout and a cached fallback; the 15 chapter globes and the interval table shipped statically; per-card error states; a status note on the About page listing the services so friends understand outages are upstream.
6. Licensing and attribution: Wikipedia text (CC BY-SA) and each Commons photo (varied) need visible credit; OSM needs ODbL attribution; some plate-reconstruction models carry non-commercial or attribution terms. Mitigation: per-card source links, per-photo credit line from extmetadata, a fixed attribution control on the map, and the About page naming the exact model used; the site is non-commercial and stays that way.
7. Privacy: typed addresses are sent to third-party services (Nominatim, Wikipedia-family) which log requests. Mitigation: state it plainly on the About page, store nothing server-side (there is no server), no analytics, geolocation strictly opt-in, recent addresses only in the visitor's own localStorage with a clear button.
8. Phone performance: MapLibre with vector tiles, a globe projection and two tile sources can stutter on older phones. Mitigation: never run globe at street zoom, fade rather than stack both bases at full opacity, lazy-load deep time, throttle network calls to snapped steps, cap photos, and test on a mid-range Android early.
9. Gesture conflicts between the tape, the sheet and the map on small screens. Mitigation: strict region ownership, touch-action rules, snapping only after the finger lifts, and the step buttons as an always-available precise alternative.
10. Scope and maintenance for a beginner owner: nine rings times six rungs times eight sources is a big matrix. Mitigation: the (ring, time) -> cards resolver keeps the logic in one place, no build step, each source is one file, and the MVP ships with four rungs and seven rings; the build order above gives a working site after every step.
11. Deep-time correctness: paleo-positions are model-dependent and uncertain, Macrostrat gives the mapped surface unit, not the bedrock under a specific house, and chapter blurbs are generalizations. Mitigation: wording like 'roughly', 'according to the X model', 'mapped rock at this spot', and a one-tap 'how sure is this?' line per deep-time card.
12. The 300,000 to 1 million years gap and the unequal chapter widths are deliberate but could confuse. Mitigation: end-cap messages on the tape and the 'shown: 750 Ma' style labels so the tape never implies precision it does not have.

concepts.angle: TIMELINE-FIRST. The product is a single horizontal time ribbon (vertical rail on wide screens) running from today back to the formation of Earth, built from seven stitched "stretches" that are each linear in their own unit (years, decades, centuries, millennia, 1-2-5 ladder, 5/10-million-year frames, 100-million-year frames) so the whole 4.5-billion-year span is about 300 snap stops. The ribbon is the only primary control: the map and the nine rings are read-only views of "this place at the stop under the playhead". The time scale also sets the default spatial scale (year stops look at the block, century stops at the city, million-year stops at the plate), so moving back in time naturally zooms the map and attention outward through the rings.
concepts.concept:
You type your address and the site drills a "core sample" straight down through time at that exact spot. Across the bottom of the phone screen there is one long ruler. Today is at the right end; drag it leftward and you pass through every year of the 1900s, then decades, then centuries, then the ice ages, then the age of dinosaurs, all the way back to the molten Earth. The ruler stretches and squeezes so that the recent past gets lots of room (one tick per year) and deep time is compressed (one tick per 100 million years), but it is still one continuous ribbon: there is never a mode switch, you just keep sliding.

Above the ruler, two things answer to wherever you have stopped. The map shows the place as it was at that date: real historical streets where someone has mapped them, a faded "ghost" of today's streets where nobody has, bare coastlines and ice for the ice ages, and a spinning globe with the continents in their old positions when you are millions of years back, with a dot showing where your house was then (it was probably under the sea, or near the equator). Below the map is a stack of cards, one per "ring": your house, your block, your street, your neighborhood, your city, your county, your state, your country, and finally the tectonic plate. Each card shows what is known about that ring at that moment. The small rings (house, block, street) are usually thin or empty, and the site is honest about that: an empty ring folds to a single grey line, and the next ring out that does have something lights up and takes over.

Rings are born over time, like tree rings. Slide back before 1821 and the Springfield card says "Springfield does not exist yet (founded 1821), this land is part of Illinois Territory". Slide back before 1776 and the country ring goes hollow too. By 10,000 BCE only the continent is left, and by 300 million years ago the only ring with a story is the plate, plus a note about how old the rock under your foundation is. Friends you share the link with land on exactly the place, date, and ring you were looking at, because all of that is in the URL.

It is a static page hosted free on GitHub Pages, with no accounts, no keys and no server of your own. Every fact comes live from public sources (OpenStreetMap, Wikipedia, OpenHistoricalMap, a plate-reconstruction service, a geology database) straight into the visitor's browser, and every card says where it came from.

screens.name: Where (address screen)
screens.description: Full-screen single input: 'Type an address, a landmark, or a town'. Controls: text field with autocomplete from the OSM geocoder (debounced 400 ms, max 5 suggestions, no fetch under 4 characters to respect the 1 request/second policy); a 'Use my location' button (browser geolocation, reverse-geocoded); three example chips the owner can edit in a config file ('Try: 221B Baker St', 'The Alamo', 'Your childhood home'). Below the field, a small animated ring glyph (nine concentric circles drawing in from the outside) that becomes the loading animation. One-line privacy note: 'Addresses are sent only to the OpenStreetMap geocoder and are not stored.' Empty/error states: 'We couldn't find that. Try adding the city or country.' and, for an address that resolves only to a town centroid, a yellow note 'We found the town but not the exact house; rings will start at Neighborhood.'

screens.name: Drilling (progressive load state of the main screen)
screens.description: Not a separate page: the main screen rendered with skeleton cards while nine fetches run in parallel. Rings fill in from the OUTSIDE in (country and state arrive in under a second from Wikipedia; city next; house/block/street last or never). The ring chips at the top turn from grey to solid as each resolves; the ribbon's event dots pop in as events are parsed. The ribbon is usable immediately at the 'Years' stretch with the ghost map; nothing blocks on the slow sources. If a source fails (CORS outage, rate limit) its ring shows 'Couldn't reach Wikipedia for this ring, tap to retry' instead of blank.

screens.name: Place in Time (main screen)
screens.description: Portrait layout top to bottom: (1) 48 px header: time-aware breadcrumb of the place ('12 Elm St · Springfield · Illinois · USA', shrinking to 'Illinois Territory', 'North America', 'Laurentia' as rings go hollow), share button, back-to-search. (2) Map pane at 38 vh, collapsible to a 96 px strip by scrolling the cards; tap to expand to full screen; shows a date badge ('Map as of 1 Jan 1871 · OpenHistoricalMap' or 'Today's streets shown as a ghost: no historical map here yet' or '150 million years ago · plate reconstruction'). (3) Ring chip row (horizontally scrollable): House, Block, Street, Neighborhood, City, County, State, Country, Plate; chip style encodes state (solid = has content at this stop, outlined = has content at other times, dotted = nothing known at all, hollow-with-year = not yet born at this stop). (4) Ring card stack, scrolling vertically, inner ring first. (5) Bottom dock, fixed, in the thumb zone: readout row (big year label such as '1871', subtitle 'Years · Springfield is 50 years old'; tap the label to open Jump), step buttons ◀ ▶ with long-press repeat, Play/Pause; then the 72 px time ribbon itself, then safe-area padding. Everything about the view (lat, lon, stop index, focused ring, map expanded or not) is in the URL hash.

screens.name: Ring Reader (full-screen ring sheet)
screens.description: Opened by tapping a ring card. Shows that one ring at the current stop at full width: title ('Springfield in the 1870s'), the matched Wikipedia paragraphs with their source section links, Commons photos dated within the window (v1.1), a 'founded / named / built' line from Wikidata or OSM tags, and two navigation rows: 'Earlier in this ring: 1865 Lincoln funeral' / 'Later in this ring: 1908 race riot' (which move the ribbon when tapped), and 'Zoom out: see Illinois at this time'. The ribbon stays visible at the bottom so time can still be scrubbed from inside the reader; the sheet content re-renders live as the playhead moves.

screens.name: Core Sample (whole-timeline overview)
screens.description: Opened from a 'See everything we found' link under the ribbon or by tapping the band label. A full-height vertical column (like a tree core or a stratigraphic column) with the seven stretches drawn proportional to their stop count, not to real elapsed time, so the 1900s are tall and the Hadean is short. Nine thin lanes left-to-right (house to plate) carry a dot for every known event, plus a horizontal 'birth' line per ring (founded/built dates) and a bracket for 'the rock under this house formed here'. Landmark labels on the right margin (1900, 1500, year 1, 10,000 BCE, Last Glacial Maximum, asteroid impact, Great Dying, first animals, Snowball Earth, oldest rocks, Earth forms). Tap anywhere to jump the ribbon there. This screen answers 'why did nothing change when I scrubbed to 1300?' at a glance: the lanes are visibly empty there.

screens.name: Map, expanded
screens.description: Full-screen map with the ribbon still docked at the bottom. Pan/zoom enabled here only (in the collapsed pane, drag is disabled so it does not trap the page scroll). Layer legend tied to the stretch: Years/Decades show the OHM historical layer over a ghost of today; Centuries/Millennia/Ice ages show land, rivers, lakes (bundled Natural Earth) with an optional ice-sheet overlay; Million years and Deep time show an orthographic globe drawn on canvas with reconstructed coastlines and the 'you were here' dot with a paleo-latitude readout. A 'Recenter on my house' button and, in deep time, a 'Show today's coastline as ghost' toggle.

screens.name: Jump to a time (sheet)
screens.description: Opened by tapping the big year readout. A number field that accepts '1954', '800 BC', '20,000 years ago', '66 Ma', '2.4 billion years ago' and snaps to the nearest stop; quick picks: 'The year I was born' (asks once, stored locally), 'When this house was built' (if known), 'When the city was founded', 'Last Ice Age (20,000 years ago)', 'Dinosaurs (100 Ma)', 'Earth forms (4.54 Ga)'. Also the seven stretch names as buttons that jump to the youngest stop of that stretch.

screens.name: About and Sources
screens.description: Static page: what the site is, the honesty rules ('faint streets are today's, not historical'; 'plate positions are a model'), per-source credits and licenses (OpenStreetMap contributors ODbL, Wikipedia CC BY-SA, OpenHistoricalMap CC0, Natural Earth public domain, Macrostrat CC-BY, PBDB CC-BY, plate model credit), a 'Fix this' link to the relevant Wikipedia/OSM/OHM edit pages so friends who know local history can add it upstream, and the owner's editable 'examples' list.

concepts.time_scale_design:
THE RIBBON. One horizontally scrolling strip (CSS overflow-x with scroll-snap-type: x mandatory, so iOS and Android handle inertia and snapping natively) with a fixed playhead at the centre of the screen. Each snap stop is a tick with its label; stretch boundaries are thick dividers with a name. Ticks within a stretch are evenly spaced in that stretch's unit, so the ribbon is piecewise-linear and globally logarithmic-ish. Pitch: 24 px per stop in Years, 32 px per stop everywhere else, 12 px dividers; total ribbon length about 8,600 px, so today-to-Earth-formation is five flicks or one tap on a stretch chip. The playhead position is converted to a stop index on scroll (no custom gesture code).

EXACT STOPS (seven stretches, youngest first; counts assume the current year is 2026, about 301 stops total):
1. YEARS: every calendar year from the current year back to 1900 (127 stops). Window = that year. Readout '1954'.
2. DECADES: 1890, 1880, ... 1500 (40 stops). Window = that decade. Readout '1880s'.
3. CENTURIES: 1400, 1300, ... 100, and 1 (15 stops). Window = that century. Readout 'the 1300s', 'the 100s', 'year 1'.
4. MILLENNIA: 1000 BCE, 2000 BCE, ... 10,000 BCE (10 stops). Window = that millennium. Readout '3000 BCE'. Landmarks drawn on the ruler: 'writing begins ~3200 BCE', 'farming begins', 'end of the Ice Age ~9700 BCE'.
5. ICE AGES (1-2-5 ladder, in years ago): 20,000; 50,000; 100,000; 200,000; 500,000; 1,000,000; 2,000,000 (7 stops). Window = from this stop back to the next older stop. Readout '50,000 years ago'. Landmarks: 'Last Glacial Maximum 20 ka', 'Homo sapiens ~300 ka', 'Ice ages begin 2.6 Ma'.
6. MILLION YEARS: 5, 10, 15, ... 65 Ma (5 Ma frames, 13 stops), then 70, 80, ... 540 Ma (10 Ma frames, 48 stops) = 61 stops. Window = plus or minus half a frame. Readout '66 million years ago' (the ruler draws named landmarks at the true dates even when they are not stops: 23 Neogene, 34, 56, 66 asteroid impact / end of dinosaurs, 145, 201, 252 Great Dying, 299, 359, 419, 444, 485, 541 first animals with shells). Plate frames exist here.
7. DEEP TIME: 600, 700, ... 4,500 Ma (100 Ma frames, 40 stops) plus a final stop 4,540 'Earth forms' (41 stops). Readout '2.4 billion years ago'. Landmarks: 635 Ediacaran, 720 Snowball Earth, 1,000 Rodinia, 1,800, 2,400 Great Oxidation, 2,500 Proterozoic begins, 3,500 earliest life, 4,000 oldest rocks / Archean, 4,540.

Each stretch has its own colour and the page background tints with it (warm white for Years, sepia for Decades/Centuries, parchment for Millennia, ice blue for Ice ages, deep green-blue for Million years, dark red to black for Deep time), so you feel the stretch change without reading.

CONTROLS. Drag/flick the ribbon; tap a tick to go there; ◀ ▶ step one stop (long-press repeats at 6 stops per second, accelerating after 2 s); Play advances 2 stops per second and pauses 400 ms at each stretch boundary with a toast naming the new stretch; stretch chips (Years · Decades · Centuries · Millennia · Ice ages · Million years · Deep time) sit above the ribbon, the active one highlighted, tap to jump to the youngest stop of that stretch; the big readout opens the Jump sheet; keyboard: left/right = one stop, shift+left/right = one stretch, Home = today, End = Earth forms. A hidden native range input mirrors the ribbon for screen readers (aria-valuetext = the readout). navigator.vibrate(10) on stretch boundaries where supported. prefers-reduced-motion turns off inertia and the globe spin.

EVENT DOTS. Each known event for this place is a small dot on the ribbon in the colour of its ring (house dots innermost at the top edge, plate dots at the bottom edge), so before scrubbing the visitor sees where the data is thick and thin. Ring birth dates (city founded, house built) are drawn as short vertical lines with a tiny ring glyph. The bedrock age range is a translucent bracket in the deep-time stretches labelled 'rock under this house formed'.
concepts.rings_design:
THE NINE RINGS AND HOW EACH IS RESOLVED. House/lot: geocoder house number + road, plus the building's OSM tags (start_date, name, levels) if the geocoder returns a building. Block: the 150 m square around the house; its only data is what the historical map tiles contain there at the current date (count and earliest date of mapped buildings, read from rendered tile features). Street: road name; a Wikipedia article exists only for famous streets, otherwise 'named after' from Wikidata when linked. Neighborhood: the geocoder's neighbourhood/suburb/quarter, matched to a Wikipedia article 'Name, City'.
