City/town, County/region, State/province, Country: geocoder fields mapped to Wikidata items (from the geocoder's extra tags, else a label search), each giving a summary, an inception date, a History section or 'History of X' article, and images. Continent/plate: continent via the country's Wikidata item, plate id and paleo-position from the plate service, bedrock unit from the geology service, fossils within 50 km from the fossil database.

ON SCREEN. A horizontally scrolling chip row (House, Block, Street, Neighborhood, City, County, State, Country, Plate) followed by a vertical card stack in the same order, inner ring first. The chip row is the ring glyph flattened: tap a chip to scroll to its card; the card in view highlights its chip. Each card has a coloured left border in its ring colour (the same colour used for its dots on the ribbon), a title that includes the time ('Illinois in the 1870s'), up to three events for the window, and a 'More' affordance opening the Ring Reader.

FOUR CARD STATES, so no card is ever blank:
1. CONTENT: events whose range overlaps the window, newest first, each with a one-line source ('Wikipedia: History of Springfield, section Civil War').
2. QUIET (ring exists, nothing in this window): one line 'Nothing recorded for the 1740s' plus two neighbour links: '◀ 1720: French fort built' and '1763: ceded to Britain ▶' that move the ribbon. This is the most common state and the neighbour links are what keep scrubbing rewarding.
3. NOT YET (stop is older than the ring's birth date): hollow card: 'Springfield does not exist yet (founded 1821). This land is part of [the innermost living outer ring], jump to 1821'. Breadcrumb at the top drops the name at the same moment. House uses the OSM start_date if present; if unknown the house card says 'We do not know when this house was built' and never claims a birth.
4. NEVER (no data at all for this ring at this place): the card folds to a single grey 18 px line 'Nothing written about Elm Street itself, see Neighborhood' and the chip goes dotted; the line stays so the stack still reads as nine rings.

FOCUS RULE (time drives attention). Each stretch has a 'home ring': Years = House (falls through to Block, Street, Neighborhood, City), Decades = Neighborhood, Centuries = City, Millennia = County/State, Ice ages = Country/Continent, Million years and Deep time = Plate. When the playhead moves, if the focused card is QUIET/NOT YET/NEVER, the stack scrolls to the innermost ring that has CONTENT (never further in than the stretch's home ring) and that chip pulses once. The visitor can override by tapping any chip; the override holds until the next stretch boundary. Inner rings that are NOT YET or NEVER are collapsed above the fold so deep-time views open directly on the Plate card.

TIME-AWARE NAMES. Where Wikidata gives a 'replaces' or 'inception' for the city/state/country, the breadcrumb and card titles switch ('Illinois Territory' before 1818); in MVP only the hollow 'not yet' form is used, former names are a later addition.
concepts.map_time_travel:
The map is a view, not a control: it re-renders when the stop changes, and its default zoom is set by the stretch (Years z17 block, Decades z15 neighbourhood, Centuries z12 city, Millennia z8 region, Ice ages z4 continent, Million years and Deep time globe). Pinch-zoom is honoured until the next stretch boundary, then the default reasserts. A date badge at the top-left of the map always states what is being drawn and from where.

YEARS and DECADES (today to 1500): two layers. Ghost layer: today's standard map tiles, desaturated and faded (100% opacity at the current year, easing to 35% by 20 stops back) with the badge 'faint streets = today, for orientation'. Historical layer: OpenHistoricalMap vector tiles filtered with the stop's date so only features whose start/end dates bracket it render, drawn in full colour on top. Where OHM has detail (parts of many big cities) streets appear and vanish as you scrub, which is the signature moment. Where OHM is empty at this zoom, the badge switches to 'No historical map here yet (help map it on OpenHistoricalMap)' and the pane shrinks to the 96 px strip automatically so the text cards get the room. The 'you' pin stays put in both cases.

CENTURIES and MILLENNIA (1500 to 10,000 BCE): OHM is used only for its historical boundary and settlement features when present; the base is a roadless, label-free land/water/rivers/lakes map built from Natural Earth GeoJSON bundled in the repo (no network). The badge says 'Coastlines approximately as today; modern roads hidden'. The pin remains.

ICE AGES (20 ka to 2 Ma): Natural Earth land plus, where a bundled simplified ice-sheet extent file exists for the Last Glacial Maximum stop, a white translucent ice overlay (one static file, shown only at the 20,000 stop; other stops show 'ice extent not shown'). Badge: 'Sea level was ~120 m lower at 20,000 years ago; coastline not adjusted'. Later addition: lowered-coastline shading.

MILLION YEARS (5 to 540 Ma): an orthographic globe drawn on a 2D canvas (d3-geo, loaded lazily on first entry to this stretch) from reconstructed coastline frames pre-generated once at build time and committed to the repo as small simplified GeoJSON files (one per 5/10 Ma frame, roughly 20 to 40 KB each, fetched on demand and cached). The 'you were here' dot comes from one live call per stop to the plate service's point-reconstruction endpoint (lat, lon, age) and is prefetched for the three neighbouring stops so scrubbing feels continuous; between fetched stops the dot interpolates. The globe rotates to keep the dot centred. A readout under the globe: 'Your house was at 23° S, about 2,800 km from where it is today' and, when the dot falls in sea on the frame, 'probably under water'. Today's coastline can be toggled as a ghost. If the plate service is unreachable: the frame still draws, the dot is replaced by a question mark at today's coordinates and the badge says 'Could not compute the past position right now'.

DEEP TIME (600 Ma to 4,540 Ma): reconstructions are unreliable or absent here, so the map stops pretending: the globe is drawn as a plain sphere in the eon's colour with no coastlines, a label 'Continents unknown at this scale', and two overlays that are real for this spot: the bedrock bracket ('the rock under this house formed between 1.1 and 1.0 billion years ago', highlighted when the playhead is inside it, from the geology service) and, at 4,540, a short 'Earth forms' animation (sphere fades from red to grey, once, respecting reduced-motion). Fossil finds within 50 km (later addition) appear as pins on the globe when their age range contains the stop.

NO HISTORICAL DATA ANYWHERE FOR THAT PLACE AND TIME: the pane never goes blank. Priority order of fallbacks is historical layer, then ghost of today with an explicit 'ghost' badge, then Natural Earth land, then plain globe. The badge text always names the fallback honestly so a 1700 view of a 1990s subdivision is never mistaken for a historical map.
concepts.mvp_cut:
The MVP is the smallest thing that gives three 'oh!' moments: streets changing as you scrub the 1900s (where OHM has them), the city and country text changing by era, and your house dot drifting across the globe.

MVP INCLUDES: Screens 'Where', 'Place in Time' (with the drilling state), 'Jump to a time' and 'About'. All seven stretches of the ribbon with all stops, chips, step buttons, readout, event dots and the stretch background tints (Play is cheap, include it). Rings: City, County, State, Country resolved via Wikidata with inception dates and era-text from the History article/section; Neighborhood if a Wikipedia article is found; House/Block/Street present as cards but only with geocoder labels, OSM start_date when present, and the honest NEVER/NOT YET states. Plate ring with the live paleo-position dot, bundled coastline frames, and the bedrock bracket from the geology service. Map: ghost layer plus OHM date-filtered layer for Years/Decades, bundled Natural Earth for Centuries through Ice ages, canvas globe for Million years and Deep time, badge in every state. Sharing via URL hash and the Web Share API. Caching of fetched text in the browser so scrubbing is instant after the first load.

DEFERRED (in order of value): (1) Core Sample overview screen; (2) Commons photos in ring cards and the Ring Reader; (3) fossil occurrences within 50 km as events and globe pins; (4) Ice-sheet overlay at 20 ka and lowered coastlines; (5) time-aware former names (Illinois Territory) and 'replaces' chains from Wikidata; (6) block-level counts from OHM tile features; (7) street 'named after'; (8) 'my birth year' quick pick; (9) PWA install and offline shell; (10) a build-time script the owner never touches that refreshes the bundled coastline frames.

BUILD SHAPE for a beginner owner: one index.html, one CSS file, a handful of ES modules, no build step, libraries from a CDN (MapLibre GL JS, d3-geo), a data/ folder of bundled GeoJSON, a config.js with the example chips and a contact line. Deploy = push to the gh-pages branch. The owner's only ongoing job is editing config.js.
concepts.risks:
DATA AND POLICY. The OSM geocoder is a shared free service with a strict usage policy (about one request per second, identifying referer, no bulk); autocomplete must be debounced and capped, and the site must never loop over many addresses. Browser-side cross-origin access to each source can be turned off or rate-limited without notice; every provider is isolated in its own module with a visible per-ring 'couldn't reach, retry' state, and the site still works with only the bundled data (ribbon, Natural Earth, globe frames). Licences differ (OSM ODbL, Wikipedia CC BY-SA, OHM CC0, Natural Earth public domain, geology and fossil services CC-BY, plate model attribution); the About page carries them all and each card names its source, which is the main obligation for a hobby site. Today's standard OSM raster tiles as the ghost layer must be used lightly (low zoom caps, no prefetch beyond the viewport) or swapped for OHM's own today-filtered tiles.

HONESTY. The two ways this site could mislead are a ghost of today's streets read as 1700, and plate positions read as fact; both are mitigated by the always-on badge wording and by the ghost layer's desaturation and opacity. Era-text extraction from Wikipedia uses year-mention heuristics and will sometimes attach a paragraph to the wrong window (a citation year, a 'rebuilt in 1990' aside in a medieval section); showing the source section link and keeping the 'From Wikipedia' prefix makes mistakes checkable, and a 'wrong era?' flag could later feed a local exclusion list.

EMPTY RINGS. For most addresses the House, Block and Street rings will be NEVER or QUIET for all of time, which is the biggest disappointment risk and exactly what the user asked to see. The design counters it with never-blank cards (neighbour links), the auto-focus rule that lights up the next ring out, the ribbon dots that show where data is thick before scrubbing, and (deferred) the Core Sample overview. Small towns outside big-city OHM coverage will have no historical map at all; the ghost badge and auto-shrinking map pane keep that from feeling broken.

TIMELINE UX. 301 stops on a phone could feel like a slot machine; the 1-2-5 and 5/10/100 Ma frames keep deep time short, the stretch chips give instant jumps, and the readout plus tinted backgrounds keep the visitor oriented. The Years stretch is 127 of 301 stops, so a flick must be able to cross it; native scroll inertia does this. Scroll-snap behaviour differs between iOS Safari and Android Chrome; the stop index must be derived from scrollLeft on scrollend/throttled scroll rather than from assumed snap targets, with a fallback timer for browsers lacking scrollend.

PERFORMANCE AND DEVICES. MapLibre with vector tiles is heavy on old phones; cap device pixel ratio at 2, limit the OHM layer to Years/Decades, and switch to the lightweight canvas renderer for older stretches. The plate service point call is per stop; prefetching only neighbours and caching keeps it to a few dozen small requests per visit. Coastline frames must be simplified at build time (target 20 to 40 KB each) or deep time will stutter on cellular.

PRIVACY AND SHARING. Friends will enter other people's addresses; the site stores nothing and says so, and the shared URL contains coordinates, which should be stated on the share sheet. GitHub Pages has no server-side rendering, so link previews use one fixed OG image and title rather than a per-place preview.
concepts.data_to_ui_mapping:
COMMON EVENT MODEL. Every source is normalised into one array of events: { ring (0 house to 8 plate), tStart, tEnd (calendar years, negative for BCE, deep time as negative millions such as -66000000), title, body, imageUrl, sourceName, sourceUrl, kind ('event' | 'birth' | 'bedrock' | 'fossil' | 'position') }. The ribbon draws dots from this array; cards filter it by ring and by the current stop's window; the Ring Reader lists it by ring; the Core Sample overview draws all of it. Time is one signed number everywhere; a time.js module owns the stop table (stop index to window start/end, label, stretch, default zoom) and the two conversions (index to t, t to nearest index).

PLACE RESOLUTION (place.js). Geocoder search returns lat, lon, address parts, osm type/id, and extra tags. Mapping: house_number + road becomes the House label; road becomes Street; neighbourhood | suburb | quarter becomes Neighborhood; city | town | village becomes City; county becomes County; state becomes State; country becomes Country. Missing parts fold their ring to NEVER. If the geocoder result is a building, a details lookup supplies start_date (a 'birth' event on the House ring), name, and levels. Each admin ring is mapped to a Wikidata item from the geocoder's wikidata/wikipedia extra tags when present, otherwise by a label search constrained by country and type.

WIKIDATA and WIKIPEDIA per ring (providers/wiki.js). Wikidata item gives: inception (P571) becomes a 'birth' event and the ring's birth line; continent (P30) and 'replaces' (P1365) for later time-aware names; image (P18) and the sitelink to the Wikipedia article. Wikipedia REST gives the summary (card header) and the 'History of X' article if it exists, else the History section of X. Era-text extraction: split into paragraphs; find year mentions (four-digit years, 'BC/BCE', 'Nth century', 'N million/billion years ago'); each paragraph becomes an event spanning the min and max years found, paragraphs without years inherit the previous paragraph's range since history sections flow chronologically; each event keeps the section anchor as sourceUrl. Cards show the events whose range overlaps the current window, trimmed to the first 60 words with 'More'.

OPENHISTORICALMAP (map.js, Years/Decades only). Vector tiles loaded in MapLibre with a filter expression that keeps features whose start_decdate and end_decdate bracket the current stop's date; the filter is updated on every stop change (no refetch). The ghost layer is a raster source underneath with opacity driven by the stop index. Block-level counts (deferred) use queryRenderedFeatures within the 150 m square.

NATURAL EARTH (bundled files, Centuries to Ice ages). 50 m land, rivers, lakes as GeoJSON in data/; drawn as a MapLibre GeoJSON source with no labels; the LGM ice-sheet file (deferred) is one more GeoJSON drawn only at the 20,000 stop.

PLATE RECONSTRUCTION (providers/plates.js, Million years and Deep time). Point endpoint: (lat, lon, age in Ma) becomes a 'position' event per stop stored in a cache keyed by stop; the globe reads it for the dot and the readout. Coastline frames: pre-generated at build time from the same service at every stop in the Million years stretch, simplified and committed as data/coast/{age}.json, fetched on demand and cached in memory. Deep time stops draw no coastlines.

GEOLOGY (providers/bedrock.js). One call with lat, lon returns the map unit with its age bounds (Ma), name and lithology; becomes one 'bedrock' event on the Plate ring spanning tEnd to tStart and a bracket on the ribbon; the Plate card shows 'Under this house: {lithology} ({unit name}), formed {b_age} to {t_age} Ma'.

FOSSILS (providers/fossils.js, deferred). Occurrences within a bounding box of about 50 km with coordinates and min/max age become 'fossil' events on the Plate ring; shown as dots and as globe pins when the stop falls within their range.

FRONT-END ARCHITECTURE. No framework and no build step: index.html, styles.css, and ES modules: time.js (stop table), place.js (geocoding and ring resolution), providers/*.js (one per source, each exporting getEvents(place) that resolves progressively and never throws to the UI), events.js (merge, index by ring and by time, memoised window queries), ribbon.js (scroll-snap ribbon, readout, stepping, play), rings.js (chip row and card stack, four card states, focus rule), map.js (layer-per-stretch switching between MapLibre and the canvas globe), router.js (URL hash of the form #/@lat,lon/t=INDEX/r=RING/m=0|1, read on load and written on every change, with pushState only on stop changes larger than one stretch so Back is useful), cache.js (in-memory plus Cache API for fetched text, with a 7-day age). Libraries from a CDN: MapLibre GL JS and d3-geo (lazy). The owner edits only config.js (example chips, radius for fossils, contact line).
concepts.mobile:
LAYOUT. Portrait phone is the primary design: header 48 px, map pane 38 vh (collapses to a 96 px strip as soon as the card stack scrolls, expands to full screen on tap), chip row 44 px, card stack fills the rest, bottom dock fixed at 40 px readout row + 72 px ribbon + env(safe-area-inset-bottom). The ribbon and step buttons live entirely in the thumb zone. All tap targets are at least 44 px. On landscape or screens wider than 900 px the same components re-flow: the ribbon becomes a vertical rail on the left (same code, rotated via a writing-mode/transform wrapper, with scroll-snap-type: y), map top-right, cards bottom-right.

GESTURES. The ribbon is a native horizontal scroller, so flicking works at full OS quality and nothing in the page intercepts touch; overscroll-behavior-x: contain keeps iOS back-swipe from firing. In the collapsed map pane, drag and pinch are disabled so the pane never traps vertical card scrolling; the expanded map has full gestures and its own close button. Long-press on ◀ ▶ uses pointer events with a repeat timer. The chip row scrolls horizontally with scroll-snap and the active chip is kept in view.

PERFORMANCE. Vector tiles only in Years/Decades; the lightweight canvas globe elsewhere; d3-geo is fetched only when a deep-time stretch is first entered; device pixel ratio capped at 2; coastline frames and ghost tiles limited to the viewport; stop changes are coalesced with requestAnimationFrame so a fast flick renders only the stops the eye can see; text fetches are cached so scrubbing back and forth never refetches. Target: first usable ribbon under 2 s on a mid-range phone on 4G, all rings resolved under 6 s.

FEEDBACK. The readout updates on every frame of the scroll, the stretch tint cross-fades over 250 ms, a short vibration marks stretch boundaries, and an aria-live region announces the readout text at a polite rate (once per 600 ms). prefers-reduced-motion disables inertia, tint fades and the globe rotation.

SHARING. The share button uses the Web Share API with the current URL and a text line like 'Springfield, Illinois in 1871 on Rings'; on desktop it copies the link. The URL carries place, stop, ring and map state so friends land on the same view. The share sheet notes that the link contains the coordinates.

DEVICE QUIRKS. scrollend is polyfilled with a 120 ms idle timer; 100vh issues are avoided with dvh units and a fixed dock; the address input uses inputmode text with autocomplete off and enterkeyhint 'search'; the Jump sheet's number field uses inputmode numeric; the page is installable later as a PWA but the MVP ships without a service worker to keep debugging simple for the owner.

scores.strengths: Zero learning curve: it is a page you scroll, which is the one gesture every phone user already knows. The first 10 seconds land hard because the one-sentence biography at the top stitches the richest facts (city founded, rock age, paleo-position) into something personal even when the house itself has nothing. Thin data is turned into the metaphor instead of a failure: thin rings look thin in the glyph, the card says what it does know and points you outward, and scrolling naturally carries you past the empty rings into the rich ones. The 'Not yet. Portland will be founded in 1851, 61 years from now' countdown is instantly understandable and funny. MVP time control (20 named Chapters plus a stepper) is the simplest of the three to grasp: tap 'Last day of the dinosaurs' and the story re-tells itself. Map captions always say whether you are looking at a faded modern map.
scores.weaknesses: Time travel is the least discoverable: a 96px collapsed sheet at the bottom is easy to miss, and the full 7-gear, 266-stop gearbox is over-engineered for a non-technical user (rollover-with-hold, Shift+arrow gears). Phone chrome is heavy before you scroll: 56px header + 180px postcard + 96px dial sheet leaves little room for the first card. The map is small, so the 'streets vanish as you scrub' moment is muted compared with the map-first concept. A lot of reading; friends who want to poke rather than read get less. Chapter cards at past dates only have dated Wikidata facts in MVP, so flipping 1890 to 1850 may change little in the middle rings.

scores.strengths: The mental model 'it is Google Maps but with a time slider' is immediately graspable, and the fly-in to your own house is a satisfying opening. The signature moments (house footprint blinking out in its build year, streets fading to ghost, border going dashed, lift-off to a globe with your house riding the continent) are the most visceral of the three. Filled/hollow/dashed dots on the ladder and tape are a smart way to steer people toward rich rings and periods. Nearest-stories-with-distances is the best empty state for the House/Street rings of any concept. Hand-written world-context JSON means the panel can never be blank. Tap-the-map to drop a pin is a great fallback.
scores.weaknesses: Too many controls to learn on a 390px screen: a Time Tape, a rung pill, magnifier buttons, pinch-on-tape to change units, a ring pill you tap or swipe, a bottom sheet with three detents. Needing three coach marks on first visit is the tell that it is not immediately understandable. The hero (the map) is the weak link for most addresses: outside a few well-mapped cities, dragging the tape in 1850 just fades today's streets, so the main screen spends most of its time in its own failure state. Text lives in a one-line peek you must drag open, so the delightful content is a gesture away. Most houses have no build date, so the house-blinks-out moment rarely fires. Gesture conflicts between tape, sheet and map are a real phone risk the concept itself flags.

scores.strengths: One continuous ruler with no mode switch is conceptually the simplest time control: drag left to go back, keep dragging, the background tint tells you which era you are in. Native scroll-snap means flicks feel like the OS, not a custom widget. The thin-data story is the strongest of the three: event dots on the ribbon show where history is thick before you scrub, QUIET cards give '1865 Lincoln funeral / 1908 race riot' neighbor links so scrubbing is always rewarding, NEVER folds to one grey line, and the focus rule lights up the next ring out when the one you are on goes hollow. Rings being 'born' over time with the breadcrumb shrinking to 'Illinois Territory' then 'Laurentia' is a lovely, understandable idea. Core Sample overview answers 'why did nothing change?' at a glance.
scores.weaknesses: The main screen is crowded on a phone: header, 38vh map, chip row, card stack, and a 112px dock leave the cards maybe a third of the screen, and the opening is skeletons that fill from the outside in, so the first thing to appear is the country, the least personal ring. 127 of 301 stops are single years where most rings are QUIET, so the first flick can feel like a slot machine of 'nothing recorded'. The focus rule auto-scrolling the card stack while you drag can be disorienting. 'Core sample' and 'stretches' are more technical metaphors than 'story' or 'map'. The Core Sample overview, the best thin-data screen, is deferred. The address screen uses autocomplete, which the OSM geocoder policy forbids, so the search box is at risk of being blocked.

judgements.graft_ideas: From the TIMELINE concept (index 2): (1) Put event dots / a thickness bar on the Time Dial and on each Chapters-list row so the reader sees where this address's history is thick before flipping back; derive them locally from the per-ring year index, no extra requests. (2) Add the QUIET card state with neighbor links at past dates ('Nothing recorded for the 1740s. ◀ 1720: French fort built | 1763: ceded to Britain ▶') that move the dial, so scrubbing is always rewarding, and the NOT-YET card's 'jump to 1851' link. (3) Tint the page background by era (warm white, sepia, parchment, ice blue, deep green-blue, red-to-black) so the time jump is felt without reading. (4) The time-aware breadcrumb in the sticky header that shrinks ('12 Elm St · Springfield · Illinois · USA' to 'Illinois Territory' to 'North America' to 'Laurentia') as rings go hollow, and the focus rule: when the dial moves and the ring you are reading goes 'Not yet', scroll to the next living ring and pulse its glyph ring. (5) When the gearbox ships in MVP+1, implement the slider as a native scroll-snap ribbon (CSS overflow-x, scroll-snap-type: x mandatory) rather than custom gesture code, and mirror it with a hidden range input for screen readers. (6) The yellow 'We found the town but not the exact house; rings start at Neighborhood' note on the Front Door, and 'Fix this' links to the Wikipedia/OSM/OHM edit pages in About. From the MAP concept (index 1): (7) 'Nearest stories' with distances (Wikipedia geosearch, 100 m house / 300 m street / 1 km neighborhood) as the thin-ring empty state, each tappable to zoom the postcard there, far better than OSM tags alone; plus Commons photos nearest the chosen year with distance and date on the expanded Chapter sheet. (8) Tap-the-map to drop a pin on the Front Door as the fallback for places without addresses, and 'Use my location'. (9) A hand-written /data/context.json (climate, people, animals by time band and continent, plus 15 chapter blurbs) so the deep-time chapters never go blank when Macrostrat or GPlates are down. (10) In the postcard, make the house footprint vanish at its build year with a 'Not built yet' label and draw admin boundaries dashed with 'border as of today' when the entity did not exist yet; recompute the ring glyph's dashed/hollow state per date. (11) A free-text 'Jump to a time' field accepting '1924', '3000 BCE', '66M', '4.5B' alongside the Chapters list. (12) Merge rings that resolve to the same entity ('City · County') instead of showing a fake level, keep Photon as a one-file swap-in geocoder if Nominatim blocks the site, and use Cache API stale-while-revalidate so revisits open instantly.

scores.strengths: Best fit between architecture and data reality: the hero is text that actually exists (city/state/country via Wikidata+Wikipedia, Macrostrat rock, bundled globe), and the map is an optional companion, so the least reliable sources (OHM coverage, house-level data) can fail without breaking the product. Explicit non-map path (Save-Data, MapLibre only loads after the first chapter renders), one map instance with cooperativeGestures, IntersectionObserver-driven per-ring fetching with a 600px margin, skeleton cards keeping ring order, system fonts, one 640px image per card with width/height set: this is a sound phone performance story. Nominatim handled correctly (submit-only, 1 req/s spacing, no autocomplete). Deep time never depends on a live service for the land: coastlines bundled for all 17 stops, GPlates only for the dot, globe still drawn on failure. d3-geo inline SVG globe is lighter and more portable than MapLibre globe projection. MVP cut is disciplined: Chapters-only dial (20 stops + stepper) instead of the 266-stop gearbox, past-date text limited to dated Wikidata facts so the heuristic chapter finder is deferred. Each data adapter fails independently and the 'thin ring'/'not yet'/'folded' states are well specified, so nothing goes blank. Hash routing works on GitHub Pages without config.
scores.weaknesses: The OHM 'count rendered features, switch to fallback if under threshold' rule requires waiting for the map 'idle' event after each date change and can flicker between modes; an always-on ghost base with a caption is simpler and equally honest. Re-rendering chapters while keeping the scroll pinned to the current ring on every date change is a real implementation subtlety (measure offsetTop before/after and compensate) that is easy to get wrong on iOS. The Wikidata P131 upward walk is sequential (4-6 hops) and P131 chains are messy in practice, so 'Hero in 2 seconds' is optimistic and the chain needs a fallback from Nominatim address parts. sessionStorage caching is per-tab and ~5MB; Cache API would persist across visits and hold large entity JSON. Vite+TypeScript adds a build step a beginner owner must keep working (mitigated by one GH Action). The custom Api-User-Agent header forces a CORS preflight on every Wikimedia call. The full gearbox (rollover hold timers, vibration, 7 gears) is deferred but as specified is custom gesture code; it should be built on native scroll-snap when it comes. Sticky chrome (56px header + 180px postcard + 96px dial) eats a lot of a small phone until the postcard collapses.

scores.strengths: Cleanest state model of the three: one {pin, rings, ringIndex, rung, time} store, URL hash as source of truth, (ring,time)->cards and (rung,time)->map-layers resolvers, one service module per source with timeout/retry/cache, Cache API stale-while-revalidate, a single request queue for Nominatim. Always-on ghost fade with a persistent Map Note is simpler and more honest than threshold switching. Per-card skeleton with an 8s timeout and 'tap to retry'. The hand-written /data/context.json world-context fallback and the 15 static chapter globes mean the panel can never be blank. Deep-time code lazy-loaded on first entry. Gesture ownership by region and touch-action rules are thought through. Tap-the-map pin drop and Photon as a one-file geocoder swap are good resilience ideas. Dark-mode map style and prefers-reduced-motion covered. No build step.
scores.weaknesses: Structurally the weakest on graceful degradation: the map IS the product, so it is WebGL-only with no non-map path; if MapLibre fails to load, WebGL is unavailable (old Android, some webviews), or tiles are slow, there is nothing to use. The hero view outside a handful of OHM-rich cities is a faded ghost of today's streets, so the signature moments mostly do not happen for the owner's friends. Ring boundaries via six Nominatim /reverse calls with polygon_geojson=1 at 1 req/s means 6+ seconds before the ladder is real, and state/country polygons from Nominatim are multi-megabyte unless polygon_threshold is used; 7 Nominatim requests per address is heavy for a hobby site under that policy. The Time Tape is custom momentum/fling/snap gesture code plus pinch-to-change-rung on a custom element, competing with browser pinch-zoom and requiring touch-action: none; this is the classic source of cross-browser bugs, and the need for coach marks is a tell. Magnetic ring snapping fights user zoom intent and triggers panel recomputation cascades. MapLibre globe projection plus two tile sources plus Macrostrat raster tiles is heavy on mid-range phones (acknowledged). Commons geosearch with extmetadata in MVP is slow (often seconds for a batch). Year-mined sentences shipped in MVP are a known accuracy risk. The bottom sheet with three detents, right-edge ladder, tape and map all share a 390px screen.

scores.strengths: The single best engineering decision in all three concepts: the ribbon is a native horizontal scroll container with scroll-snap-type: x mandatory, so inertia and snapping are OS-quality with zero custom gesture code, the stop index is derived from scrollLeft on scrollend (with a timer polyfill), and a hidden native range input mirrors it for screen readers. The normalised event model ({ring, tStart, tEnd, kind, source}) feeding cards, ribbon dots, Ring Reader and overview makes scrubbing pure local filtering after the first load, so hundreds of stops cost no network. Map is a view not a control; collapsed pane has drag disabled so it never traps scroll; explicit fallback priority (historical -> ghost -> Natural Earth -> plain globe) with an always-on badge. Canvas globe via lazily loaded d3-geo, coastline frames pre-simplified to 20-40KB each, GPlates point prefetched for neighbouring stops with interpolation. Outside-in progressive load so country/state appear first. Four card states plus neighbour links keep QUIET windows rewarding. No build step, config.js only, device pixel ratio capped at 2, rAF-coalesced stop changes.
scores.weaknesses: Nominatim autocomplete (debounced, 4+ chars, 5 suggestions) directly violates Nominatim's usage policy, which forbids client-side autocomplete regardless of debouncing; as written this can get the site's IP blocked. The hero control's payoff depends on event density, and for most addresses the Years stretch (127 of 301 stops) is QUIET at House/Block/Street, so the auto-focus rule is doing heavy lifting; timeline-first exposes the data thinness more than story-first does. MVP ships the era-text heuristic (paragraph year-mining of History sections) for all admin rings, which is the most error-prone piece. Front-loading nine fetches including full History articles is heavier on initial load than lazy per-ring fetching. Updating OHM filters across ~100 style layers plus ghost opacity on every snapped stop during a flick needs careful rAF coalescing to avoid jank. Rotating the ribbon into a vertical rail with a CSS transform is a footgun (transforms do not change the scroll axis); it needs a real vertical layout. Using tile.openstreetmap.org raster tiles as the ghost layer is subject to OSM's tile usage policy (they flag it, but the fix should be default). Focus rule auto-scrolling the card stack on playhead moves risks feeling jumpy.

judgements.graft_ideas: 1) From concept 2: when the full Time Dial gearbox is built (MVP+1), implement the per-gear slider as a native horizontal scroll container with scroll-snap-type: x mandatory and a fixed playhead, deriving the stop index from scrollLeft on scrollend (120ms idle-timer polyfill), with a hidden native <input type=range> mirrored for screen readers (aria-valuetext = readout). Drop the custom slider, 300ms hold-to-rollover and pinch logic; gears become stretch dividers on one ribbon. 2) From concept 2: adopt the normalised event model ({ring, tStart, tEnd, kind: event|birth|bedrock|fossil|position, title, body, sourceName, sourceUrl}) as the single structure behind story.ts. Chapters, the tree-ring glyph thickness, 'not yet' states, the 'rock forming now' callout and dial/Chapters-list teasers all become local filters over one array, so re-telling the biography for a new date never refetches. Add the QUIET state with neighbour links ('< 1865: ... / 1908: ... >') for rings that exist but have nothing at the chosen date, and small per-ring event dots on the dial so readers see where data is thick before scrubbing. 3) From concept 1: replace the threshold-based OHM/fallback switch with an always-on ghost base whose opacity is a function of the date (e.g. 0.55 at 1950, 0.25 at 1800, 0 by 10,000 BCE) plus a persistent Map Note chip; keep queryRenderedFeatures only to choose the caption wording after the map 'idle' event, never to toggle layers. Cheap wow moments worth keeping on the postcard: the house footprint vanishing in its build year with a 'Not built yet' label, and the ring outline going dashed with 'border as of today' before the entity's inception. 4) From concept 1: ship a hand-written /data/context.json (climate, people, animals per time band and continent, plus 15-20 chapter blurbs) as the floor for 'The land' and 'Life here then', so deep-time and pre-contact chapters are never empty; add the one-tap 'how sure is this?' line on deep-time cards; swap sessionStorage for Cache API stale-while-revalidate keyed by request URL (persists across visits, no 5MB cap); use an 8-second skeleton timeout per card with 'Couldn't reach Wikipedia, tap to retry'; keep Photon as a one-file drop-in if Nominatim ever blocks; add 'tap the map to drop a pin' on the Front Door for places without addresses (one Nominatim reverse call). 5) From both: a free-text 'Jump to a time' field that parses '1954', '800 BC', '20,000 years ago', '66 Ma', '2.4 billion years ago' and snaps to the nearest stop, sitting above the Chapters list; prefetch the GPlates dot for the neighbouring stops and interpolate between them; tint the page background per gear so the stretch change is felt without reading. 6) Also lift concept 2's explicit map fallback ladder (historical OHM -> ghost today -> bundled Natural Earth -> plain globe) into the postcard caption logic, and its outside-in load order (country/state/city resolve and render first, house/block last) for the initial Hero.
